Cardiac hemangioma.description: A rare benign vascular tumor of the heart composed of abnormal blood-filled vascular channels. It may arise in the myocardium, including the left ventricle, and can be incidentally discovered.

Cardiac fibroma.description: A benign primary cardiac tumor composed predominantly of dense fibroblastic and collagenous tissue. It usually occurs in the ventricular myocardium and can be found incidentally, although it is more common in children.

Cardiac myxoma.description: The most common benign primary cardiac tumor, usually arising from the interatrial septum in the left atrium. It can cause obstruction, embolic events, or constitutional symptoms, but may occasionally be asymptomatic.

Cardiac lipoma.description: A benign tumor composed of mature adipose tissue that may arise in the subendocardium, myocardium, or pericardium. Many cardiac lipomas are incidentally identified and asymptomatic.

Cardiac thrombus.description: An intracardiac blood clot, usually associated with atrial fibrillation, ventricular dysfunction, myocardial infarction, ventricular aneurysm, or hypercoagulable states. A left ventricular thrombus typically forms in areas of impaired wall motion.

Splenic infarction.description: Ischemic necrosis of splenic tissue caused by impaired splenic arterial or venous blood flow; imaging commonly shows peripheral wedge-shaped, poorly perfused splenic lesions.

Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection with spl.normalized_text: Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection with splenic infarction
Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection with spl.description: A respiratory infection caused by Mycoplasma pneumoniae that can rarely produce hypercoagulability, vascular thrombosis, and splenic infarction as extrapulmonary complications.

Splenic abscess.description: A localized infection within the spleen, usually bacterial, which can cause fever, inflammatory marker elevation, and left upper quadrant pain; ultrasound may show focal hypoechoic splenic lesions.

Community-acquired left lower lobe pneum.normalized_text: Community-acquired left lower lobe pneumonia with referred abdominal pain
Community-acquired left lower lobe pneum.description: Infection of the lower lung can irritate the diaphragm and present with upper abdominal pain, fever, cough, sputum production, and pleuritic pain.

Amoebic liver abscess (Entamoeba histoly.description: A hepatic abscess caused by invasive Entamoeba histolytica infection, often occurring weeks to years after travel to an endemic region. It commonly causes fever, leukocytosis, and right upper abdominal or pleuritic diaphragmatic pain; bowel symptoms may be mild or absent.

Pyogenic liver abscess.description: A localized bacterial infection of the liver, commonly caused by enteric organisms such as Klebsiella pneumoniae, Escherichia coli, streptococci, or anaerobes. It produces fever and inflammatory-marker elevation and may cause diaphragmatic pain when located near the liver capsule.

Melioidosis with hepatic abscess (Burkho.normalized_text: Melioidosis with hepatic abscess (Burkholderia pseudomallei infection)
Melioidosis with hepatic abscess (Burkho.description: Melioidosis is an infection caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, endemic in northern Australia and parts of Southeast Asia. It can cause pneumonia, sepsis, and internal abscesses involving the liver and spleen; incubation may range from days to years.

Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome (perihepatitis.normalized_text: Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome (perihepatitis associated with pelvic inflammatory disease)
Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome (perihepatitis.description: Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome is inflammation of the liver capsule, usually caused by Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae in association with pelvic inflammatory disease. It causes sharp pleuritic upper abdominal pain, often with fever.

Acute bacterial gastroenteritis with rea.normalized_text: Acute bacterial gastroenteritis with reactive systemic inflammation
Acute bacterial gastroenteritis with rea.description: An invasive bacterial intestinal infection, such as Salmonella, Campylobacter, or Shigella infection, can cause fever, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, neutrophilia, and systemic myalgia. Some pathogens can rarely lead to extraintestinal infection including hepatic abscess formation.

OPA1-related dominant optic atrophy plus.normalized_text: OPA1-related dominant optic atrophy plus syndrome (DOA+)
OPA1-related dominant optic atrophy plus.description: A mitochondrial disorder caused by pathogenic OPA1 variants, typically producing slowly progressive bilateral optic atrophy and sometimes additional neurologic features including spastic paraplegia, sensory disturbance, ataxia, neuropathy, deafness, or cognitive impairment.

Primary progressive multiple sclerosis.description: A chronic inflammatory demyelinating disorder of the central nervous system that can cause gradually progressive spastic paraparesis, sensory symptoms, and bladder dysfunction, often with oligoclonal bands in CSF.

Hereditary spastic paraplegia with optic.normalized_text: Hereditary spastic paraplegia with optic atrophy (complex hereditary spastic paraplegia, including SPG7 or related forms)
Hereditary spastic paraplegia with optic.description: A group of inherited neurodegenerative disorders characterized by progressive lower-limb spasticity; complex forms may also cause optic atrophy, sensory abnormalities, urinary dysfunction, ataxia, neuropathy, and cognitive features.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder.description: An autoimmune inflammatory disorder that commonly causes optic neuritis and myelitis, leading to visual loss, sensory symptoms, spasticity, and bladder dysfunction; many cases are associated with aquaporin-4 antibodies.

Leber hereditary optic neuropathy with n.normalized_text: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy with neurologic involvement (LHON-plus)
Leber hereditary optic neuropathy with n.description: A maternally inherited mitochondrial disorder that primarily causes bilateral optic neuropathy and can occasionally be accompanied by movement disorders, peripheral neuropathy, myelopathy, or MS-like neurologic manifestations.

Wilson disease (hepatolenticular degener.description: An autosomal-recessive ATP7B disorder causing impaired biliary copper excretion, copper accumulation in the liver, brain, and cornea, and progressive hepatic, neurologic, hematologic, and endocrine manifestations.

Herb-induced liver injury with cholestat.normalized_text: Herb-induced liver injury with cholestatic hepatitis
Herb-induced liver injury with cholestat.description: Liver injury caused by herbal or traditional medicines, often presenting with cholestasis, jaundice, pruritus, and sometimes impaired hepatic synthetic function.

Autoimmune hepatitis.description: An immune-mediated inflammatory liver disease that can occur in children and adolescents and may lead to jaundice, chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, and impaired liver synthetic function.

Progressive familial intrahepatic choles.normalized_text: Progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis or other inherited cholestatic liver disease
Progressive familial intrahepatic choles.description: A group of genetic disorders causing impaired bile formation or transport, leading to childhood or adolescent cholestasis, severe pruritus, jaundice, and progressive liver disease.

Azathioprine hypersensitivity syndrome.description: An acute systemic drug-hypersensitivity reaction to azathioprine, typically occurring within days to weeks of starting treatment and causing fever, malaise, rash, arthralgia, and inflammatory-marker elevation.

Drug-induced Sweet syndrome (acute febri.normalized_text: Drug-induced Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis)
Drug-induced Sweet syndrome (acute febri.description: A neutrophilic inflammatory skin disorder that may be triggered by medications, including azathioprine, and commonly presents with fever, painful erythematous plaques or nodules, arthralgia, and neutrophilia.

Serum sickness-like reaction due to azat.normalized_text: Serum sickness-like reaction due to azathioprine
Serum sickness-like reaction due to azat.description: A medication-related immune reaction characterized by fever, rash, malaise, and polyarthralgia, usually arising one to two weeks after exposure to a new drug.

Erythema nodosum.description: An inflammatory panniculitis causing painful erythematous nodules, usually on the lower legs, often accompanied by fever, arthralgia, and elevated inflammatory markers; it can be triggered by drugs, infection, or autoimmune disease.

Traumatic retropharyngeal hematoma.description: Bleeding into the retropharyngeal/prevertebral soft tissues after neck trauma, which can expand and compress the pharynx and upper airway.

Blunt laryngeal trauma with laryngeal ed.normalized_text: Blunt laryngeal trauma with laryngeal edema or hematoma
Blunt laryngeal trauma with laryngeal ed.description: Injury to the larynx after blunt anterior neck trauma, causing soft-tissue swelling, vocal-cord dysfunction, hematoma, and possible airway obstruction.

Cervical spine injury with associated pr.normalized_text: Cervical spine injury with associated prevertebral soft-tissue hematoma
Cervical spine injury with associated pr.description: A cervical vertebral fracture or ligamentous injury may cause bleeding and swelling in the prevertebral/retropharyngeal space, sometimes producing dysphagia and airway compression.

Pancreatic insulinoma.description: A usually benign pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor that autonomously secretes insulin, causing recurrent fasting hypoglycemia. It classically produces Whipple triad: symptoms of hypoglycemia, low measured glucose, and improvement after glucose intake.

Endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia.description: A biochemical syndrome of hypoglycemia caused by inappropriate internal insulin secretion, most commonly due to insulinoma, but potentially due to other causes such as diffuse beta-cell hyperfunction.

Non-insulinoma pancreatogenous hypoglyce.description: Diffuse pancreatic beta-cell hyperfunction causing excessive insulin release and hypoglycemia. In adults it is less common than insulinoma and may occur after gastrointestinal surgery, though it can be idiopathic.

Factitious hypoglycemia due to sulfonylu.normalized_text: Factitious hypoglycemia due to sulfonylurea or meglitinide exposure
Factitious hypoglycemia due to sulfonylu.description: Hypoglycemia caused by ingestion of insulin-secretagogue medications, which stimulate endogenous pancreatic insulin release and therefore produce elevated insulin and C-peptide levels.

Exogenous insulin-induced hypoglycemia.description: Hypoglycemia caused by administration of insulin from an external source, either accidental or intentional. Laboratory testing typically shows high insulin with suppressed endogenous C-peptide.

Adrenal insufficiency.description: Deficient cortisol production, due to adrenal or pituitary disease, which can impair glucose maintenance and cause fatigue, weakness, and sometimes hypoglycemia.

Slipping rib syndrome (interchondral sub.normalized_text: Slipping rib syndrome (interchondral subluxation of a false rib)
Slipping rib syndrome (interchondral sub.description: Hypermobility or subluxation of the anterior cartilaginous portion of a lower false rib, usually ribs 8-10, causing intermittent sharp lower chest or upper abdominal wall pain from intercostal nerve irritation. Dynamic ultrasound may demonstrate abnormal movement of the involved rib cartilage.

Intercostal muscle strain.description: Overuse or partial injury of the muscles between the ribs, often following new or intense exercise, twisting, forceful breathing, or core training.

Costochondritis.description: Inflammation or irritation of costochondral or chondrosternal junctions that causes localized chest-wall pain, often worsened by movement, deep inspiration, or palpation.

Rib stress injury or stress fracture.normalized_text: Rib stress injury or stress fracture
Rib stress injury or stress fracture.description: A repetitive-load injury to a rib that can occur in athletes after a sudden increase in training volume or intensity, producing focal pain that worsens with activity.

Abdominal rectus or external oblique mus.normalized_text: Abdominal rectus or external oblique muscle strain
Abdominal rectus or external oblique mus.description: Overuse injury of the anterior abdominal-wall musculature, commonly associated with forceful trunk flexion, rotation, or high-intensity core exercises.

Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not other.normalized_text: Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not otherwise specified (CEL-NOS)
Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not other.description: A clonal myeloid neoplasm characterized by persistent marked eosinophilia, abnormal eosinophil precursors or blasts, dysplastic hematopoiesis, and often cytogenetic abnormalities. It can cause pulmonary eosinophilic infiltration and respiratory symptoms.

Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophi.normalized_text: Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophilia and tyrosine-kinase gene rearrangement (such as PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1, or PCM1-JAK2 rearrangement)
Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophi.description: A group of clonal hematologic neoplasms in which a kinase-gene rearrangement drives eosinophil proliferation. These disorders may involve blood, bone marrow, lungs, skin, heart, or other organs and can mimic allergic asthma or eosinophilic pneumonia.

Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia.description: An eosinophilic lung disease causing subacute cough, dyspnea, blood eosinophilia, and pulmonary opacities due to eosinophil accumulation in lung tissue. It is often associated with asthma but generally responds dramatically to systemic corticosteroids.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyang.description: A systemic eosinophilic vasculitis usually associated with adult-onset asthma, eosinophilia, sinus disease, pulmonary infiltrates, neuropathy, skin lesions, and possible cardiac or renal involvement.

diagnoses.name: Mixed-cellularity subtype of classic Hodgkin's lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: Mixed-cellularity subtype of classic Hodgkin's lymphoma

Anaplastic large cell lymphoma, ALK-posi.description: An aggressive CD30-positive T-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that commonly occurs in children and may cause systemic symptoms, lymphadenopathy, extranodal abdominal disease, and inflammatory laboratory abnormalities.

Classical Hodgkin lymphoma.description: A B-cell lymphoma characterized by inflammatory symptoms and often painless lymph-node enlargement; advanced disease can produce constitutional symptoms, anemia, and extranodal involvement.

Burkitt lymphoma.description: A rapidly growing high-grade B-cell lymphoma in children that frequently involves the abdomen, particularly the ileocecal region, and may cause bowel symptoms, bleeding, obstruction, and systemic illness.

Crohn disease.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract and commonly causes abdominal pain, diarrhea, gastrointestinal bleeding, growth failure, inflammation, and iron-deficiency anemia in children.

Disseminated histoplasmosis.description: A systemic fungal infection caused by Histoplasma species, which can occur after exposure in endemic areas and may cause prolonged fever, weight loss, anemia, abdominal symptoms, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenic involvement, and elevated inflammatory markers.

Plasmodium falciparum malaria.description: Severe mosquito-borne malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum, which can produce high parasitemia, intravascular hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury, jaundice, and multiorgan dysfunction. The travel history, malaria rapid test, and blood smear showing ring forms are highly supportive.

Severe falciparum malaria with blackwate.normalized_text: Severe falciparum malaria with blackwater fever
Severe falciparum malaria with blackwate.description: A severe hemolytic manifestation of falciparum malaria characterized by massive intravascular hemolysis, hemoglobinuria causing dark urine, jaundice, and potentially acute renal failure.

Leptospirosis.description: A zoonotic spirochetal infection acquired through exposure to water or soil contaminated with animal urine. Severe disease can cause fever, headache, jaundice, acute kidney injury, thrombocytopenia, and dark urine.

Dengue fever.description: A mosquito-borne viral illness that commonly causes high fever, headache, gastrointestinal symptoms, thrombocytopenia, and elevated liver enzymes. Severe dengue can cause plasma leakage, bleeding, and organ dysfunction.

Acute viral hepatitis A or E.normalized_text: Acute viral hepatitis A or E
Acute viral hepatitis A or E.description: Food- and water-associated viral hepatitis causing fever, malaise, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, jaundice, dark urine, and elevated aminotransferases. Hepatitis E is particularly relevant after travel to endemic regions.

Delayed esophageal perforation from cerv.normalized_text: Delayed esophageal perforation from cervical spine hardware erosion
Delayed esophageal perforation from cerv.description: A late complication of anterior cervical spine fixation in which plates or screws erode into or perforate the pharynx/esophagus, causing leakage, infection, and possible fistula formation.

Descending necrotizing mediastinitis.description: A severe infection of the mediastinum that spreads downward from a neck, pharyngeal, esophageal, or cervical-spine source and can produce pus collections in the chest.

Cervical spinal instrumentation infectio.normalized_text: Cervical spinal instrumentation infection with paraspinal abscess
Cervical spinal instrumentation infectio.description: Infection involving prior cervical fusion hardware and surrounding soft tissues, producing a deep paraspinal abscess that may spread into the retropharyngeal space, esophagus, or mediastinum.

Retropharyngeal/deep neck space abscess.description: A collection of pus in the deep fascial spaces of the neck that can cause painful swallowing and may extend into the mediastinum through the danger space.

Esophagomediastinal fistula secondary to.normalized_text: Esophagomediastinal fistula secondary to infected cervical hardware
Esophagomediastinal fistula secondary to.description: An abnormal communication between the esophagus and mediastinal infected space, often caused by perforation from cervical instrumentation, allowing saliva and bacteria to contaminate the mediastinum.

Boerhaave syndrome (spontaneous esophage.description: A full-thickness rupture of the esophagus, usually in the distal left posterolateral esophagus, caused by a sudden increase in intrathoracic pressure after forceful vomiting. It causes mediastinal air, pleural contamination, and may rapidly progress to sepsis.

Mallory-Weiss tear.description: A mucosal laceration at the gastroesophageal junction caused by retching or vomiting, typically producing upper gastrointestinal bleeding rather than a full-thickness esophageal perforation.

Acute coronary syndrome.description: Myocardial ischemia caused by reduced coronary blood flow, commonly presenting with pressure-like chest pain, diaphoresis, nausea, and vomiting.

Acute aortic dissection.description: A tear in the aortic intima allowing blood to dissect through the aortic wall, often causing abrupt severe tearing chest pain that radiates to the back.

Psychogenic nonepileptic seizures (funct.description: Paroxysmal episodes that resemble epileptic seizures but are not caused by epileptic cortical discharges; they are commonly associated with psychological trauma, PTSD, depression, anxiety, and other functional neurologic symptoms.

Generalized tonic-clonic epilepsy.description: Epileptic seizures characterized by abrupt loss of consciousness, tonic stiffening followed by rhythmic clonic jerking, and a postictal recovery period. They may be primary generalized or focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizures.

Focal epilepsy with focal-to-bilateral t.normalized_text: Focal epilepsy with focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizures
Focal epilepsy with focal-to-bilateral t.description: Seizures beginning in one brain region, sometimes with an aura, that spread to produce bilateral tonic-clonic convulsions. Focal seizures can be associated with sensory, visual, autonomic, cognitive, or emotional symptoms before convulsions.

Convulsive syncope.description: Transient loss of consciousness caused by reduced cerebral blood flow, often due to vasovagal episodes or cardiac arrhythmia. Brief tonic or myoclonic jerks can occur during syncope and may mimic epilepsy.

Incarcerated right obturator hernia caus.normalized_text: Incarcerated right obturator hernia causing small-bowel obstruction
Incarcerated right obturator hernia caus.description: A pelvic hernia in which small bowel protrudes through the obturator canal. It classically occurs in thin, elderly, multiparous women and may cause bowel obstruction with pain radiating to the medial thigh or knee (Howship-Romberg sign).

Incarcerated femoral hernia causing smal.normalized_text: Incarcerated femoral hernia causing small-bowel obstruction
Incarcerated femoral hernia causing smal.description: A femoral hernia occurs when bowel passes through the femoral canal below the inguinal ligament. It is more common in older women and can become incarcerated or strangulated, causing bowel obstruction.

Incarcerated inguinal hernia causing sma.normalized_text: Incarcerated inguinal hernia causing small-bowel obstruction
Incarcerated inguinal hernia causing sma.description: An inguinal hernia is protrusion of abdominal contents through the inguinal canal. If bowel becomes trapped, it may cause acute intestinal obstruction and potentially ischemia.

Susac syndrome.description: A rare autoimmune endotheliopathy causing microvascular occlusion in the brain, retina, and inner ear. It classically presents with encephalopathy or headache, branch retinal artery occlusions, and sensorineural hearing loss; corpus callosum lesions are characteristic on MRI.

Multiple sclerosis.description: An immune-mediated demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that commonly affects young women and can cause recurrent neurologic deficits, optic neuritis, sensory symptoms, and characteristic white-matter MRI lesions.

Systemic lupus erythematosus with retina.normalized_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus with retinal vasculopathy/antiphospholipid-associated retinal vascular occlusion
Systemic lupus erythematosus with retina.description: Systemic autoimmune disease and/or antiphospholipid syndrome can cause arterial thrombosis, retinal vascular occlusions, central nervous system ischemia, headache, and neurologic symptoms in young women.

Neuro-Behçet disease with retinal vascul.description: Behçet disease is a systemic inflammatory vasculitis that may cause recurrent ocular inflammation and retinal vascular disease, neurologic involvement, headache, and occasionally auditory symptoms.

Myofibrillar myopathy (desmin-related my.description: A hereditary muscle disease caused by disruption of myofibrillar structural proteins, often including desmin. It can produce progressive axial/paraspinal and proximal weakness, elevated CK, muscle biopsy protein aggregates, and cardiac conduction abnormalities.

Myofibrillar myopathy due to MYOT mutati.normalized_text: Myofibrillar myopathy due to MYOT mutation (myotilinopathy)
Myofibrillar myopathy due to MYOT mutati.description: An autosomal-dominant myofibrillar myopathy caused by MYOT mutations. It usually begins in adulthood with slowly progressive distal, proximal, or axial muscle weakness, elevated CK, and protein aggregates on muscle biopsy; some affected families have bent-spine syndrome.

Myofibrillar myopathy due to LDB3/ZASP m.normalized_text: Myofibrillar myopathy due to LDB3/ZASP mutation (ZASP-related myopathy)
Myofibrillar myopathy due to LDB3/ZASP m.description: A late-onset inherited myofibrillar myopathy caused by LDB3/ZASP variants, characterized by progressive muscle weakness, axial involvement or camptocormia, CK elevation, and sometimes cardiac arrhythmia or cardiomyopathy.

Mitochondrial myopathy with ataxia and s.normalized_text: Mitochondrial myopathy with ataxia and sensorineural hearing loss
Mitochondrial myopathy with ataxia and s.description: Mitochondrial disorders can cause a combination of myopathy, exercise intolerance or weakness, cerebellar dysfunction, sensorineural hearing loss, cognitive changes, and cardiac rhythm abnormalities. The phenotype may be caused by mitochondrial DNA or nuclear-gene defects.

diagnoses.name: B-cell lymphoma, unclassifiable, with features intermediate between diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: B-cell lymphoma, unclassifiable, with features intermediate between diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma
diagnoses.icd11_title: B-cell lymphoma unclassifiable with features intermediate between Burkitt lymphoma and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

Burkitt lymphoma/leukemia.description: An aggressive mature B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that may involve lymph nodes, extranodal soft tissue, bone marrow, and peripheral blood. It typically shows a mature clonal B-cell phenotype with surface immunoglobulin expression and often CD10 positivity.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.description: A mature aggressive B-cell lymphoma composed of large transformed B cells. It can present with nodal or extranodal masses but is substantially less common than Burkitt lymphoma in very young children.

B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma.description: A malignancy of immature B-cell precursors that commonly presents in children with marrow involvement, anemia, lymphadenopathy, bone pain, or soft-tissue masses. Typical cells express precursor markers such as TdT and often CD34.

High-grade B-cell lymphoma, not otherwis.normalized_text: High-grade B-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified
High-grade B-cell lymphoma, not otherwis.description: An aggressive mature B-cell lymphoma with clinical and immunophenotypic features overlapping Burkitt lymphoma and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. It may present with extranodal disease, nodal enlargement, marrow involvement, and circulating lymphoma cells.

Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis due to Sch.normalized_text: Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis due to Schistosoma mansoni
Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis due to Sch.description: Chronic S. mansoni infection can cause intestinal disease and egg-induced periportal hepatic fibrosis (Symmers pipestem fibrosis), leading to hepatosplenomegaly and portal hypertension while liver function may initially remain preserved.

Intestinal schistosomiasis.description: Intestinal infection with S. mansoni results from deposition of parasite eggs in the bowel wall, producing chronic inflammation, abdominal discomfort, diarrhoea, and sometimes blood loss or colonic polyps.

Pyogenic liver abscess.description: A pyogenic liver abscess is a bacterial collection within the liver that commonly causes persistent fever, right upper-quadrant pain, and focal hepatic abnormalities on ultrasound or CT.

Traumatic hepatic hematoma or liver cont.normalized_text: Traumatic hepatic hematoma or liver contusion
Traumatic hepatic hematoma or liver cont.description: Blunt abdominal trauma can produce liver contusion or hematoma, presenting with right upper-quadrant pain and a focal hepatic lesion on imaging.

diagnoses.name: ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction
diagnoses.icd11_title: Acute ST segment elevation myocardial infarction

Acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial i.description: Acute myocardial infarction caused by abrupt coronary artery occlusion, with ECG findings suggesting anterior/anterolateral myocardial injury, typically involving the left anterior descending artery.

Polycythemia vera.description: A JAK2-associated myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by increased red-cell mass and often elevated platelets and leukocytes; it can cause aquagenic pruritus and arterial thrombosis, including coronary thrombosis.

Essential thrombocythemia.description: A chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm causing persistent platelet elevation and increased risk of arterial or venous thrombosis; some patients have microvascular symptoms or bleeding.

Acute coronary syndrome due to coronary.normalized_text: Acute coronary syndrome due to coronary thrombosis associated with a myeloproliferative neoplasm
Acute coronary syndrome due to coronary.description: Acute coronary ischemia may occur when hypercoagulability from a myeloproliferative neoplasm, such as polycythemia vera or essential thrombocythemia, causes in-situ coronary thrombosis despite few traditional atherosclerotic risk factors.

Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) o.description: Acid reflux or esophageal inflammation can cause burning substernal discomfort and may improve with antacids or proton-pump inhibitors, but it does not explain ischemic ECG changes or troponin elevation.

Pulmonary sequestration (likely left low.normalized_text: Pulmonary sequestration (likely left lower-lobe intralobar or extralobar sequestration)
Pulmonary sequestration (likely left low.description: A congenital nonfunctioning segment of lung tissue that lacks normal bronchial communication and receives systemic arterial blood supply, usually from the aorta. It may cause neonatal respiratory distress and can appear as an abnormal lower-lung opacity or hyperlucent region depending on associated air trapping.

Congenital pulmonary airway malformation.normalized_text: Congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM), possibly a CPAM-sequestration hybrid lesion
Congenital pulmonary airway malformation.description: A developmental malformation of the lower respiratory tract characterized by cystic or overexpanded abnormal lung tissue. Hybrid lesions can have features of both CPAM and pulmonary sequestration, including systemic arterial supply from the aorta.

Congenital lobar overinflation (congenit.description: A congenital disorder in which a lung lobe becomes progressively overexpanded because of impaired bronchial cartilage support or partial airway obstruction. The overinflated lobe may compress adjacent lung and shift the mediastinum, causing neonatal respiratory distress.

Neonatal pneumothorax, including tension.description: Air in the pleural space can collapse a lung and cause acute hypoxemia, hypotension, and cardiorespiratory instability. It may occur after positive-pressure ventilation and can produce unilateral hyperlucency with mediastinal shift.

Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy with sev.normalized_text: Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy with severe perinatal asphyxia
Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy with sev.description: Brain injury caused by impaired oxygen delivery and blood flow around the time of birth. Severe cases present with profound depression at delivery, prolonged resuscitation, metabolic instability, and may be treated with therapeutic hypothermia.

Complement-mediated thrombotic microangi.normalized_text: Complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy (atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome)
Complement-mediated thrombotic microangi.description: A complement-dysregulation disorder causing endothelial injury, thrombosis in renal microvasculature, severe hypertension, acute kidney injury, and variable hemolysis. It may be triggered by cocaine use, infection, or other physiologic stressors and can have familial predisposition.

Cocaine-associated thrombotic microangio.description: Cocaine can cause severe vasoconstriction, endothelial injury, malignant hypertension, and thrombotic microangiopathy, leading to acute renal failure and microangiopathic hemolysis. Cocaine may also uncover an underlying complement-mediated disorder.

Malignant hypertension-associated thromb.description: Severely elevated blood pressure can injure renal arterioles and glomerular capillaries, causing fibrinoid vascular injury, microangiopathic hemolysis, rapidly progressive renal failure, and hypertensive encephalopathy.

Hepatitis C-associated membranoprolifera.normalized_text: Hepatitis C-associated membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (often cryoglobulinemic glomerulonephritis)
Hepatitis C-associated membranoprolifera.description: Chronic hepatitis C can cause immune-complex glomerulonephritis, frequently with mixed cryoglobulinemia. It commonly produces proteinuria, hematuria, hypertension, kidney dysfunction, and complement consumption.

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP.description: TTP is a thrombotic microangiopathy, usually caused by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency, characterized by thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, neurologic abnormalities, renal injury, and sometimes fever.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.normalized_text: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) with area postrema syndrome
Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.description: An autoimmune astrocytopathy associated with aquaporin-4 antibodies that can involve the area postrema in the dorsal medulla, causing intractable nausea and vomiting, and may also cause brainstem, spinal cord, and optic nerve deficits.

Multiple sclerosis with brainstem involv.description: A chronic immune-mediated demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that can produce brainstem signs, pyramidal weakness, nystagmus, and sensory or motor deficits. Severe isolated intractable vomiting is less characteristic.

Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein anti.normalized_text: Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease (MOGAD) with brainstem encephalitis
Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein anti.description: An inflammatory demyelinating disorder associated with MOG antibodies that may affect the optic nerves, spinal cord, brainstem, or brain and can occasionally cause vomiting and other brainstem symptoms.

Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae infective e.description: A rare bacterial infection of heart valves caused by Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, a Gram-positive rod with characteristic intrinsic resistance to vancomycin and frequent involvement of the aortic valve.

Enterococcus faecalis infective endocard.description: Subacute infection of a native or prosthetic heart valve caused by Enterococcus faecalis, commonly producing prolonged constitutional symptoms and a new or worsening regurgitant murmur.

Viridans-group streptococcal native-valv.description: A typically subacute bacterial endocarditis occurring on previously abnormal native valves, often associated with fatigue, fever, arthralgia, and progressive valvular regurgitation.

Staphylococcus aureus infective endocard.description: An invasive bacterial infection of heart valves that may cause fever, systemic symptoms, valvular destruction, vegetations, and acute or worsening regurgitation.

Venous air embolism with paradoxical sys.normalized_text: Venous air embolism with paradoxical systemic air embolism through a patent foramen ovale
Venous air embolism with paradoxical sys.description: Air introduced during venesection can enter the venous circulation, obstruct the pulmonary vasculature, and cross a patent foramen ovale into the arterial circulation, causing cerebral and coronary air embolism.

Pulmonary air embolism.description: Air entering the venous system travels to the right heart and pulmonary arteries, where it can obstruct pulmonary blood flow and cause acute respiratory and cardiovascular symptoms.

Paradoxical cerebral air embolism causin.normalized_text: Paradoxical cerebral air embolism causing transient ischemic attack
Paradoxical cerebral air embolism causin.description: Venous air can cross a right-to-left intracardiac shunt, such as a patent foramen ovale, enter the cerebral arterial circulation, and produce transient focal neurological deficits.

Paradoxical coronary air embolism causin.normalized_text: Paradoxical coronary air embolism causing acute myocardial ischemia
Paradoxical coronary air embolism causin.description: Air crossing a patent foramen ovale may enter the coronary arteries and transiently obstruct coronary blood flow, producing acute coronary syndrome-like chest pain, ECG changes, and troponin elevation.

Pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma (PXA), WHO.description: A rare, typically superficial astrocytic glioma that often occurs in younger patients, frequently involves the temporal lobe, presents with seizures, and commonly harbors a BRAF V600E mutation.

Anaplastic pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma.normalized_text: Anaplastic pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma (PXA with anaplastic features)
Anaplastic pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma.description: A more aggressive form of PXA, currently classified as a higher-grade tumor when there is increased mitotic activity and/or necrosis; it may retain BRAF V600E mutation and can recur after an initially lower-grade PXA diagnosis.

Ganglioglioma.description: A usually slow-growing mixed neuronal-glial tumor that commonly arises in the temporal lobe and is a well-known cause of chronic focal epilepsy; some cases carry BRAF V600E mutations.

Dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor (.description: A benign, epilepsy-associated glioneuronal tumor, usually cortical and temporal-lobe based, most often presenting with longstanding seizures in children or young adults.

Dermatomyositis.description: An idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by symmetric proximal muscle weakness and distinctive cutaneous findings, including heliotrope rash and Gottron papules/sign.

Clinically amyopathic dermatomyositis wi.normalized_text: Clinically amyopathic dermatomyositis with evolving myositis
Clinically amyopathic dermatomyositis wi.description: A dermatomyositis-spectrum disorder in which characteristic skin manifestations may precede the development of clinically significant muscle inflammation and weakness.

Polymyositis.description: An inflammatory myopathy causing subacute, symmetric proximal skeletal muscle weakness, usually without the characteristic skin findings of dermatomyositis.

Antisynthetase syndrome.description: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy syndrome that can include myositis, interstitial lung disease, inflammatory arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, mechanic's hands, fever, and occasionally dermatomyositis-like rashes.

Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy.description: A severe autoimmune myopathy characterized by rapidly progressive symmetric proximal weakness and muscle necrosis, often associated with markedly elevated muscle enzymes and sometimes statin exposure or autoantibodies.

Phenytoin-induced osteomalacia.description: Defective bone mineralization caused by long-term phenytoin use, often through accelerated vitamin D metabolism leading to vitamin D deficiency, hypocalcemia or hypophosphatemia, secondary hyperparathyroidism, and insufficiency fractures.

Vitamin D deficiency osteomalacia.description: Osteomalacia due to inadequate vitamin D availability, causing impaired calcium and phosphate mineralization of bone, diffuse bone pain, muscle weakness, and insufficiency fractures.

Hypophosphatemic osteomalacia.description: A metabolic bone disorder caused by chronic phosphate depletion, which may be inherited, medication-related, or tumor-induced; it produces defective mineralization, bone pain, weakness, and pseudofractures.

Osteoporosis with insufficiency fracture.description: Reduced bone mass and structural bone deterioration that predispose to fragility fractures, particularly in postmenopausal women. Insufficiency fractures can cause focal bone pain.

Skeletal metastatic disease.description: Cancer spread to bone can cause multifocal bone pain, pathologic fractures, and increased uptake on bone scintigraphy or PET imaging, potentially mimicking metabolic bone disease.

Group A streptococcal infective endocard.normalized_text: Group A streptococcal infective endocarditis of the mitral valve
Group A streptococcal infective endocard.description: Infection of the endocardial surface of the heart, usually involving a valve, with formation of vegetations. In this case, positive group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal blood cultures, a mitral-area systolic murmur, and echocardiographic vegetation strongly support mitral-valve infective endocarditis.

Acute ischemic stroke due to septic cere.normalized_text: Acute ischemic stroke due to septic cerebral embolism
Acute ischemic stroke due to septic cere.description: An ischemic stroke caused by embolization of infected valvular material from infective endocarditis into a cerebral artery. The brain image is consistent with an acute focal cerebral infarction, likely embolic in this clinical setting.

Acute severe mitral regurgitation with c.normalized_text: Acute severe mitral regurgitation with congestive heart failure secondary to infective endocarditis
Acute severe mitral regurgitation with c.description: Mitral-valve infection can damage valve leaflets or chordae, causing severe mitral regurgitation. The resulting volume overload may produce left-sided heart failure and pulmonary congestion.

Splenic infarction or splenic abscess fr.normalized_text: Splenic infarction or splenic abscess from septic embolization
Splenic infarction or splenic abscess fr.description: Infective endocarditis can cause systemic emboli to the spleen, producing splenic infarction and, when infected, a splenic abscess. The abdominal ultrasound image appears compatible with a focal splenic lesion in the setting of endocarditis.

Cranioectodermal dysplasia (Sensenbrenne.description: A rare autosomal-recessive ciliopathy characterized by sagittal craniosynostosis/dolichocephaly, distinctive facial appearance, skeletal abnormalities, ectodermal defects involving hair, teeth and nails, and progressive renal disease often leading to chronic kidney failure.

Schimke immuno-osseous dysplasia.description: A rare inherited disorder caused by SMARCAL1-related dysfunction, featuring progressive nephropathy, skeletal dysplasia with short stature, characteristic facies, sparse hair, and variable cellular immunodeficiency with recurrent infections.

Mainzer-Saldino syndrome.description: A skeletal ciliopathy characterized by renal disease, cone-shaped epiphyses and phalangeal abnormalities, retinal dystrophy, and variable short stature or thoracic skeletal abnormalities.

Dermatomyositis, likely malignancy-assoc.description: An inflammatory autoimmune myopathy characterized by proximal muscle weakness, markedly elevated muscle enzymes, and distinctive cutaneous findings such as Gottron papules. In adults, especially men over 50, it may be associated with an underlying cancer.

Esophageal carcinoma associated with par.normalized_text: Esophageal carcinoma associated with paraneoplastic dermatomyositis
Esophageal carcinoma associated with par.description: Esophageal cancer can trigger paraneoplastic dermatomyositis, in which an immune response associated with the tumor causes inflammatory muscle disease and characteristic skin lesions.

Polymyositis.description: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy causing symmetric proximal muscle weakness, dysphagia, and elevated creatine kinase; unlike dermatomyositis, it does not usually cause a characteristic rash.

Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy.description: A severe autoimmune muscle disease characterized by rapidly progressive proximal weakness and very high creatine kinase levels, sometimes associated with cancer, statin exposure, or specific autoantibodies.

Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease.description: Childhood idiopathic osteonecrosis of the femoral head, leading to collapse, fragmentation, remodeling, and possible deformity of the hip joint.

Slipped capital femoral epiphysis.description: Displacement of the femoral-head growth plate relative to the femoral neck, usually occurring in adolescents during growth spurts and often associated with obesity.

Transient synovitis of the hip.description: A self-limited inflammatory hip synovitis in children, often causing acute or subacute hip pain, limp, and reduced range of motion.

Septic arthritis of the hip.description: A bacterial infection of the hip joint that typically produces acute severe pain, inability to bear weight, fever, and systemic illness; it requires urgent treatment.

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis involving.normalized_text: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis involving the hip
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis involving.description: A chronic inflammatory arthritis beginning before age 16 that can cause joint pain, stiffness, limping, and restricted range of motion.

Gas-forming pyogenic liver abscess.description: A bacterial infection within the liver forming an abscess, sometimes containing gas produced by organisms such as Klebsiella pneumoniae or anaerobic bacteria. It can mimic pneumoperitoneum on an erect chest radiograph.

Pyogenic liver abscess without emphasis.normalized_text: Pyogenic liver abscess without emphasis on gas formation
Pyogenic liver abscess without emphasis.description: A localized collection of pus in the liver caused by bacterial infection, commonly presenting with fever, right upper quadrant pain, systemic inflammation, and sepsis.

Subphrenic abscess.description: An infected collection beneath the diaphragm, often following abdominal infection or surgery, which may cause upper abdominal pain, fever, and apparent gas under the diaphragm.

Perforated hollow viscus with pneumoperi.description: Perforation of the stomach, duodenum, bowel, or another hollow abdominal organ releases free intraperitoneal air and can cause peritonitis and sepsis.

Cri-du-chat syndrome (5p deletion syndro.description: A chromosomal disorder caused by deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5, classically associated with a high-pitched cat-like cry, microcephaly, global developmental delay, hypotonia, characteristic facial features, and occasional congenital heart defects.

Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome.description: A developmental disorder caused by deletion of chromosome 4p, usually characterized by severe growth and developmental delay, microcephaly, hypotonia, seizures, distinctive craniofacial features, and congenital malformations including cardiac defects.

1p36 deletion syndrome.description: A chromosome deletion syndrome involving the terminal short arm of chromosome 1, causing developmental delay or intellectual disability, hypotonia, microcephaly, visual abnormalities, congenital heart disease, and sometimes seizures.

Congenital cytomegalovirus infection.description: A congenital viral infection that may cause microcephaly, developmental delay, hypotonia, hearing impairment, visual abnormalities, and intracranial abnormalities such as calcifications or ventriculomegaly.

diagnoses.name: Primary yolk sac tumor of intestine
diagnoses.normalized_text: Primary yolk sac tumor of intestine
diagnoses.icd11_title: Yolk sac tumour, unspecified site, female

Primary extragonadal yolk sac tumor of t.normalized_text: Primary extragonadal yolk sac tumor of the jejunum
Primary extragonadal yolk sac tumor of t.description: A malignant germ-cell tumor producing alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) that arises outside the gonads; rare primary intestinal cases can involve the jejunum and infiltrate the full bowel wall.

Jejunal adenocarcinoma with yolk-sac-lik.normalized_text: Jejunal adenocarcinoma with yolk-sac-like or hepatoid differentiation
Jejunal adenocarcinoma with yolk-sac-lik.description: A very rare AFP-producing intestinal adenocarcinoma that may show gland-forming morphology and yolk-sac or hepatocellular-like differentiation, resulting in elevated AFP.

Abdominal Burkitt lymphoma or other non-.normalized_text: Abdominal Burkitt lymphoma or other non-Hodgkin lymphoma involving the small bowel
Abdominal Burkitt lymphoma or other non-.description: Pediatric non-Hodgkin lymphoma can present as a rapidly growing intestinal mass with abdominal pain, ascites, and mesenteric or retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy.

Small-bowel gastrointestinal stromal tum.description: A mesenchymal tumor arising from interstitial cells of Cajal that can occur in the small intestine and form a transmural bowel-wall mass, although it is uncommon in children.

Meckel diverticulum with ectopic gastric.normalized_text: Meckel diverticulum with ectopic gastric mucosa and ulcerative bleeding
Meckel diverticulum with ectopic gastric.description: A congenital ileal diverticulum that may contain acid-secreting gastric mucosa, causing adjacent ileal ulceration, significant painless or painful lower gastrointestinal bleeding, anemia, and occasionally inflammation or obstruction. The nuclear medicine appearance is consistent with ectopic gastric mucosa.

Intussusception.description: Telescoping of one segment of bowel into another, usually ileocolic in infants, causing intermittent severe colicky abdominal pain, bowel ischemia, and bloody mucus-containing stools.

Enteric duplication cyst containing ecto.normalized_text: Enteric duplication cyst containing ectopic gastric mucosa
Enteric duplication cyst containing ecto.description: A congenital duplication of the gastrointestinal tract that can contain gastric mucosa, leading to acid-related ulceration, gastrointestinal bleeding, abdominal pain, obstruction, or an abdominal mass.

Midgut volvulus due to intestinal malrot.normalized_text: Midgut volvulus due to intestinal malrotation
Midgut volvulus due to intestinal malrot.description: Twisting of the midgut around its mesenteric blood supply, usually related to congenital malrotation, causing intermittent or acute bowel obstruction and potentially life-threatening intestinal ischemia with bleeding.

Food protein-induced allergic proctocoli.description: A non-IgE-mediated inflammatory reaction to dietary proteins, commonly cow's milk or soy protein, that causes rectal bleeding in otherwise well young infants.

diagnoses.name: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia
diagnoses.normalized_text: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia
diagnoses.icd11_title: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia

Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocr.normalized_text: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia (DIPNECH)
Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocr.description: A rare pulmonary disorder, predominantly affecting older nonsmoking women, in which neuroendocrine cells proliferate in the small airways and may cause constrictive bronchiolitis. CT commonly shows multiple small pulmonary nodules with mosaic attenuation from air trapping.

Constrictive bronchiolitis (bronchioliti.description: A small-airway disorder characterized by inflammatory and fibrotic narrowing of bronchioles, producing fixed airflow obstruction and air trapping. It may be idiopathic or associated with autoimmune disease, inhalational exposure, infection, transplantation, or DIPNECH.

Pulmonary carcinoid tumors associated wi.normalized_text: Pulmonary carcinoid tumors associated with neuroendocrine-cell proliferation
Pulmonary carcinoid tumors associated wi.description: Pulmonary carcinoid tumors are well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumors that can occur as one or more pulmonary nodules. In the setting of multiple nodules, mosaic attenuation, and obstruction in an older nonsmoking woman, they may represent tumorlets/carcinoids associated with DIPNECH.

Asthma with small-airway involvement.description: Asthma is an inflammatory airway disease causing variable airflow obstruction, wheeze, dyspnea, and sometimes CT air trapping. Late-onset asthma can occur in older adults.

Chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis wit.description: An immune-mediated lung disease caused by repeated inhalation of an antigen, often producing dyspnea, cough, small-airway obstruction, mosaic attenuation, and air trapping. Fibrotic forms may also show interstitial abnormalities.

Castleman disease (hyaline vascular type.normalized_text: Castleman disease (hyaline vascular type) with pulmonary involvement
Castleman disease (hyaline vascular type.description: Castleman disease is a rare lymphoproliferative disorder characterized by enlarged lymph nodes with distinctive follicular and vascular histology. The hyaline vascular type is often localized, may cause long-standing waxing and waning lymphadenopathy, and can rarely be associated with inflammatory or granulomatous pulmonary lesions.

Pulmonary tuberculosis.description: Pulmonary tuberculosis is a mycobacterial infection that commonly causes chronic cough, fever, hemoptysis, upper-lobe infiltrates or cavitation, and granulomatous inflammation.

Sarcoidosis.description: Sarcoidosis is a systemic inflammatory disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas, most often involving the lungs and intrathoracic lymph nodes, with possible peripheral lymphadenopathy.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis.description: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is an ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis that can cause necrotizing granulomatous lung inflammation, pulmonary nodules or cavitation, hemoptysis, and systemic inflammation.

Hodgkin lymphoma.description: Hodgkin lymphoma is a lymphoid malignancy that commonly presents in young adults with painless rubbery lymphadenopathy, often in cervical or supraclavicular nodes, and may produce constitutional inflammatory symptoms and elevated soluble IL-2 receptor.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopat.normalized_text: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) due to JC polyomavirus
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopat.description: A severe opportunistic demyelinating brain infection caused by JC polyomavirus reactivation in immunosuppressed individuals. Natalizumab exposure, high anti-JCV antibody index, and subsequent fingolimod-associated lymphopenia are important risk factors.

Multiple sclerosis relapse.description: An acute or subacute episode of new inflammatory demyelination in a patient with multiple sclerosis, causing focal neurologic deficits such as visual, motor, sensory, or coordination abnormalities.

Posterior reversible encephalopathy synd.description: A clinicoradiologic syndrome of vasogenic edema, usually affecting posterior brain regions, often associated with hypertension, renal dysfunction, cytotoxic or immunosuppressive drugs, and causing seizures and visual disturbances.

Classic Fabry disease.description: An X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficient alpha-galactosidase A activity due to pathogenic GLA variants, resulting in globotriaosylceramide accumulation in vascular, neural, renal, cardiac, skin, and ocular tissues.

Fabry cardiomyopathy.description: Cardiac involvement of Fabry disease caused by glycosphingolipid accumulation in cardiomyocytes and vascular tissue, commonly producing left ventricular hypertrophy, repolarization abnormalities, arrhythmias, microvascular angina, and later fibrosis or heart failure.

Fabry nephropathy.description: Renal involvement in Fabry disease caused by glycosphingolipid deposition in podocytes, tubular epithelial cells, endothelial cells, and vascular smooth muscle, leading to proteinuria, progressive chronic kidney disease, and potentially kidney failure.

Infected intrahepatic hematoma.description: Secondary bacterial infection of a traumatic liver hematoma, potentially progressing to an abscess or sepsis.

Pyogenic liver abscess.description: A localized bacterial collection of pus within the liver, which may arise from infection of a pre-existing traumatic hematoma.

Post-traumatic biloma with secondary inf.description: A collection of leaked bile caused by traumatic injury to intrahepatic bile ducts; it can become infected and cause systemic inflammatory findings.

Acute cholangitis.description: Bacterial infection of the biliary tree, usually associated with biliary obstruction or injury to bile ducts.

Catheter-related bloodstream infection o.normalized_text: Catheter-related bloodstream infection or ICU-acquired sepsis
Catheter-related bloodstream infection o.description: A hospital-acquired bloodstream infection, often related to central venous catheters or other invasive devices, causing fever and leucocytosis in ICU patients.

Acute generalized exanthematous pustulos.normalized_text: Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP) induced by iodinated contrast media
Acute generalized exanthematous pustulos.description: A severe acute drug-induced pustular eruption characterized by abrupt onset of numerous sterile non-follicular pustules, usually with neutrophilic inflammation. Iodinated radiographic contrast is a recognized trigger.

Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) or TEN-.normalized_text: Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) or TEN-like drug eruption due to iodinated contrast
Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) or TEN-.description: A life-threatening severe cutaneous adverse drug reaction with widespread keratinocyte necrosis, epidermal detachment, bullae, and often mucosal involvement. Rarely, lesions may have a pustular or AGEP-overlap appearance.

Generalized pustular psoriasis.description: A severe inflammatory psoriasis variant causing widespread sterile pustules on erythematous skin, often associated with systemic symptoms and neutrophilia. It may be triggered by medications, infections, or withdrawal of systemic corticosteroids.

Subcorneal pustular dermatosis (Sneddon-.description: A chronic relapsing sterile pustular dermatosis characterized by flaccid superficial pustules, usually affecting flexural and intertriginous areas and often occurring in older adults.

Capnocytophaga canimorsus fulminant seps.normalized_text: Capnocytophaga canimorsus fulminant sepsis with purpura fulminans
Capnocytophaga canimorsus fulminant seps.description: A severe zoonotic bloodstream infection caused by Capnocytophaga canimorsus, a gram-negative rod found in dog saliva. It can cause rapidly progressive septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, skin necrosis, and purpura fulminans, particularly in people with heavy alcohol use, liver disease, or impaired splenic function.

Necrotizing soft-tissue infection.description: A rapidly progressive bacterial infection of fascia, subcutaneous tissue, or muscle that causes tissue ischemia, necrosis, systemic toxicity, and potentially septic shock. It may follow traumatic wounds or animal bites and can be polymicrobial or caused by organisms such as streptococci, clostridia, or gram-negative bacteria.

Purpura fulminans due to disseminated in.normalized_text: Purpura fulminans due to disseminated intravascular coagulation
Purpura fulminans due to disseminated in.description: Purpura fulminans is a life-threatening thrombotic skin syndrome, usually triggered by overwhelming sepsis, in which disseminated intravascular coagulation causes widespread microvascular thrombosis, purpura, skin necrosis, and possible limb ischemia.

Pasteurella multocida infection after do.normalized_text: Pasteurella multocida infection after dog bite
Pasteurella multocida infection after do.description: Pasteurella multocida is a gram-negative coccobacillus commonly transmitted through dog or cat bites. It usually causes rapidly developing cellulitis and wound infection but can occasionally cause bacteremia and severe sepsis in medically vulnerable individuals.

diagnoses.name: MELAS syndrome
diagnoses.icd11_title: MELAS - [Mitochondrial encephalopathy with lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes] syndrome

MELAS syndrome (mitochondrial encephalom.normalized_text: MELAS syndrome (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes) due to MT-TL1 m.3303C>T mutation
MELAS syndrome (mitochondrial encephalom.description: A mitochondrial disorder, most often caused by pathogenic variants in the mitochondrial tRNA leucine 1 gene (MT-TL1), characterized by mitochondrial myopathy, lactic acidosis, neurologic deterioration, and recurrent stroke-like episodes at a young age.

Mitochondrial myopathy caused by an MT-T.normalized_text: Mitochondrial myopathy caused by an MT-TL1 mutation
Mitochondrial myopathy caused by an MT-T.description: A group of neuromuscular disorders caused by impaired mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, producing progressive exercise intolerance, weakness, hypotonia, muscle wasting, and lactic acid elevation. MT-TL1 mutations can produce isolated myopathy or overlap syndromes such as MELAS.

Cardioembolic ischemic stroke associated.normalized_text: Cardioembolic ischemic stroke associated with mitochondrial cardiomyopathy or intracardiac thrombus
Cardioembolic ischemic stroke associated.description: An ischemic stroke caused by embolization of thrombotic material from the heart. Mitochondrial disease can involve the myocardium and predispose to cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, ventricular dysfunction, and intracardiac thrombus formation.

Primary angiitis of the central nervous.normalized_text: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system or systemic vasculitis with cerebral involvement
Primary angiitis of the central nervous.description: Inflammatory vascular disorders can cause cerebral arterial narrowing or occlusion and ischemic stroke in young adults. They are considered in young patients with stroke and abnormal vascular imaging, although supporting inflammatory or autoimmune evidence is usually present.

Extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.description: Adenocarcinoma arising from the bile ducts outside the liver that causes progressive biliary obstruction, cholestasis, and jaundice. Imaging and pathology are consistent with an obstructing biliary mass with malignant gland-forming cells in a desmoplastic stroma.

Distal bile duct adenocarcinoma.description: A subtype of extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma arising in the distal common bile duct, often producing obstructive jaundice and biliary dilation; it can resemble pancreatic head cancer clinically and radiographically.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma of the.normalized_text: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma of the pancreatic head
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma of the.description: A malignant tumor of the pancreatic ducts that can obstruct the distal common bile duct, causing painless or minimally painful jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, anorexia, and elevated CA 19-9.

Gallbladder carcinoma with biliary obstr.description: An adenocarcinoma arising from the gallbladder that may invade or compress the extrahepatic bile ducts and produce obstructive jaundice. It generally occurs in older patients and may cause right upper quadrant pain.

Gallstone ileus due to cholecystoenteric.normalized_text: Gallstone ileus due to cholecystoenteric fistula
Gallstone ileus due to cholecystoenteric.description: Mechanical intestinal obstruction caused by a gallstone entering the bowel through an abnormal fistula between the gallbladder and intestine; the stone may migrate distally and rarely reach the rectum.

Cholecystocolonic fistula with distal pa.normalized_text: Cholecystocolonic fistula with distal passage of a gallstone
Cholecystocolonic fistula with distal pa.description: An abnormal communication between the gallbladder and colon that permits gallstones to pass directly into the large bowel, occasionally causing colonic or rectal obstruction.

Crohn's disease with enterobiliary fistu.description: Crohn's disease can cause transmural bowel inflammation and fistulas; in rare circumstances, fistulization involving the biliary system may allow gallstone migration into the gastrointestinal tract.

Acute lateral patellar dislocation.description: Displacement of the patella to the outside of the knee, commonly occurring in adolescents and often associated with generalized joint hypermobility.

Osteochondral fracture with intra-articu.normalized_text: Osteochondral fracture with intra-articular loose body after patellar dislocation
Osteochondral fracture with intra-articu.description: A fracture involving articular cartilage and underlying bone, often from the medial patella or lateral femoral condyle after a patellar dislocation; the fragment may detach and become a loose body in the joint.

Medial patellofemoral ligament injury fo.normalized_text: Medial patellofemoral ligament injury following patellar dislocation
Medial patellofemoral ligament injury fo.description: Sprain, partial tear, or tear of the medial patellofemoral ligament, the main soft-tissue restraint preventing lateral patellar displacement; it is commonly injured during lateral patellar dislocation.

Graham-Little-Piccardi-Lassueur syndrome.description: A rare variant of lichen planopilaris characterized by cicatricial scalp alopecia, non-scarring alopecia of axillary/pubic hair, and widespread follicular keratotic or spiny papules on the trunk and extremities.

Lichen planopilaris.description: An inflammatory lymphocytic disorder targeting hair follicles that causes perifollicular scale, itching, and permanent scarring alopecia; Graham-Little syndrome is a clinical variant.

Follicular lichen planus.description: A follicular form of lichen planus in which lichenoid inflammation affects follicular openings, producing rough keratotic papules and sometimes associated scarring alopecia.

Keratosis pilaris.description: A common benign follicular keratinization disorder causing small rough follicular papules, most often on the upper arms, thighs, buttocks, and sometimes trunk.

Complement-mediated atypical hemolytic u.description: A thrombotic microangiopathy, often triggered by pregnancy or preeclampsia, characterized by complement dysregulation causing microvascular thrombosis, hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and severe kidney injury.

Malignant hypertension-associated thromb.description: Severe, sustained hypertension can damage small vessels and produce endothelial injury, renal ischemia, hemolysis with schistocytes, thrombocytopenia, and progressive kidney failure.

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP.description: A life-threatening thrombotic microangiopathy caused by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency, leading to platelet-rich microthrombi, hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and variable neurologic and renal involvement.

Pregnancy-associated thrombotic microang.normalized_text: Pregnancy-associated thrombotic microangiopathy following severe preeclampsia/HELLP-spectrum disease
Pregnancy-associated thrombotic microang.description: Preeclampsia and HELLP syndrome can cause endothelial injury with hypertension, proteinuria, thrombocytopenia, hemolysis, and kidney injury; persistent disease after delivery may reveal an underlying complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy.

Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome (.normalized_text: Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome (CAPS) or antiphospholipid-associated thrombotic microangiopathy
Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome (.description: An autoimmune thrombotic disorder causing widespread small-vessel thrombosis that can affect kidneys, skin, blood counts, and pregnancy outcomes; it is usually associated with positive antiphospholipid antibodies.

diagnoses.name: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of unspecified gastrointestinal sites

Small-intestinal gastrointestinal stroma.description: A mesenchymal tumor of the gastrointestinal tract arising from interstitial cells of Cajal or related precursor cells. Ileal GISTs commonly harbor activating KIT mutations, including exon 11 deletions, and can cause occult or overt gastrointestinal bleeding.

Small-intestinal adenocarcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the small intestine that may cause bleeding, anemia, obstruction, abdominal pain, or metastatic disease. It is usually a mucosal lesion rather than a KIT-mutated mesenchymal wall-based tumor.

Small-intestinal neuroendocrine tumor (i.description: A usually slow-growing neuroendocrine neoplasm that commonly occurs in the distal ileum. It may present with abdominal pain, obstruction, mesenteric desmoplasia, or metastatic liver disease; bleeding can occur but is less characteristic.

Small-intestinal lymphoma.description: A lymphoid malignancy involving the small bowel that can present with abdominal pain, weight loss, anemia, bleeding, obstruction, or bowel-wall thickening. It typically has lymphoid histology and does not carry activating KIT mutations characteristic of GIST.

diagnoses.name: Malignant gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Malignant GIST - [gastrointestinal stromal tumour] of large intestine

Pancreatic acinar cell carcinoma.description: A rare malignant exocrine pancreatic tumor composed of acinar-type cells that produce digestive enzymes. It often presents as a large, well-circumscribed pancreatic mass in older adults and may cause nonspecific gastrointestinal symptoms.

Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor.description: A neoplasm arising from pancreatic endocrine cells. Nonfunctioning tumors can become large before detection and commonly present with abdominal fullness, a palpable mass, or nonspecific digestive symptoms.

Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pa.normalized_text: Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pancreas
Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pa.description: A typically low-grade malignant pancreatic neoplasm that is often large and well circumscribed, with mixed solid and hemorrhagic or degenerative areas. It occurs predominantly in young women but can rarely occur in older men.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.description: The most common pancreatic malignancy, arising from ductal epithelium. It usually causes obstructive jaundice, weight loss, abdominal or back pain, and is often infiltrative rather than a large circumscribed mass.

Hailey-Hailey disease (familial benign c.description: An autosomal-dominant acantholytic skin disorder caused by ATP2C1 mutations, producing recurrent painful, pruritic, eroded or crusted plaques in flexural areas. Heat, sweating, and friction commonly trigger flares.

Darier disease (keratosis follicularis).description: An inherited acantholytic keratinization disorder caused by ATP2A2 mutations, usually characterized by greasy crusted keratotic papules in seborrheic and flexural areas, often worsened by heat and sweating.

Pemphigus vegetans.description: A rare flexural variant of pemphigus vulgaris in which painful flaccid blisters evolve into vegetating, eroded, malodorous plaques, often involving the axillae and groin.

Acanthosis nigricans with secondary inte.description: A velvety hyperpigmented thickening of flexural skin, often associated with obesity and insulin resistance; friction, moisture, and secondary infection can cause intertrigo with odor and maceration.

Candidal intertrigo.description: A yeast infection of moist skin folds causing erythema, maceration, fissuring, soreness, and sometimes malodor; obesity and warm weather increase risk.

Myositis ossificans circumscripta.description: A benign, localized heterotopic bone-forming lesion within soft tissue or muscle, often developing after trauma but sometimes occurring without a recognized injury. Imaging commonly shows peripheral, zonal calcification/ossification without destruction of adjacent bone.

Extraskeletal osteosarcoma.description: A rare malignant mesenchymal tumor that produces osteoid or bone in soft tissue without direct origin from bone. It may appear as a painful enlarging mineralized soft-tissue mass.

Extraskeletal chondrosarcoma.description: A malignant cartilage-producing tumor arising in soft tissues, sometimes in the pelvis or proximal limbs. It can form a slowly enlarging painful mass with stippled, ring-and-arc, or peripheral calcifications.

Calcified soft-tissue hematoma.description: An organized hematoma can present as a painful soft-tissue mass and may develop peripheral calcification or ossification over time, particularly after trauma, surgery, anticoagulation, or bleeding disorders.

Ovarian mature cystic teratoma (dermoid.description: A common benign ovarian germ-cell tumor in young women that may contain fat, calcification, teeth, or bone. It can present as a palpable pelvic mass with pain or tenderness, especially if large or complicated by torsion.

Stiff-person syndrome (SPS), likely auto.description: A rare autoimmune neurologic disorder characterized by progressive axial and proximal limb rigidity, painful stimulus-sensitive muscle spasms, and hyperexcitability of motor pathways; often associated with anti-GAD65 antibodies and may respond to IVIG and benzodiazepines.

Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigid.normalized_text: Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM)
Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigid.description: A severe stiff-person-spectrum disorder, often associated with glycine-receptor antibodies, featuring rigidity, painful spasms, myoclonus, exaggerated startle, autonomic dysfunction, and possible brainstem or respiratory involvement.

Glycine receptor antibody-associated sti.normalized_text: Glycine receptor antibody-associated stiff-person spectrum disorder
Glycine receptor antibody-associated sti.description: An autoimmune neurologic hyperexcitability disorder associated with antibodies to glycine receptors. It may present with severe stiffness, stimulus-sensitive spasms, hyperreflexia, exaggerated startle, and respiratory or bulbar involvement; it overlaps clinically with PERM.

Hereditary spastic paraplegia.description: A group of genetic disorders causing slowly progressive bilateral lower-extremity spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, gait difficulty, and eventual mobility impairment due to corticospinal-tract dysfunction.

Tetanus.description: A toxin-mediated neurologic illness caused by Clostridium tetani, producing generalized rigidity, painful reflex spasms, hyperreflexia, and potentially life-threatening respiratory muscle involvement.

Takayasu arteritis.description: A chronic large-vessel vasculitis affecting the aorta and its major branches, often causing carotid or subclavian stenosis/occlusion in younger women. Reduced cerebral and scalp perfusion can cause syncope, stroke, and ischemic scalp ulceration.

Severe atherosclerotic carotid and great.normalized_text: Severe atherosclerotic carotid and great-vessel occlusive disease
Severe atherosclerotic carotid and great.description: Progressive narrowing or occlusion of the carotid, brachiocephalic, or subclavian arteries due to atherosclerosis. Severe disease may impair cerebral and external carotid circulation, causing collapse, stroke, and scalp ischemia.

Giant cell arteritis with scalp ischemia.normalized_text: Giant cell arteritis with scalp ischemia/necrosis
Giant cell arteritis with scalp ischemia.description: A granulomatous vasculitis of medium and large arteries, especially temporal and extracranial carotid branches. Severe inflammation can cause scalp tenderness, ulceration, or necrosis and may lead to ischemic neurologic complications.

Subclavian steal syndrome or brachioceph.normalized_text: Subclavian steal syndrome or brachiocephalic artery stenosis
Subclavian steal syndrome or brachioceph.description: Stenosis of the proximal subclavian or brachiocephalic artery can divert blood away from cerebral circulation through collateral pathways, causing vertebrobasilar insufficiency and episodes of presyncope or syncope.

Visceral leishmaniasis (Leishmania infan.description: A systemic protozoal infection transmitted by sandflies, endemic in the Mediterranean region. It is more severe in patients receiving immunosuppressive therapy, including anti-TNF agents. The smear image is consistent with intracellular Leishmania amastigotes.

Mixed cryoglobulinemic vasculitis.description: An immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis caused by circulating cryoglobulins, often associated with autoimmune disease, chronic infection, or lymphoproliferative disorders.

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or lu.normalized_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or lupus-like autoimmune syndrome
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or lu.description: A systemic autoimmune disease characterized by autoantibody production, immune-complex formation, hypocomplementemia, cytopenias, arthritis, and cutaneous vascular manifestations. Anti-TNF therapy can rarely induce a lupus-like syndrome.

Felty syndrome.description: A complication of long-standing seropositive rheumatoid arthritis characterized by neutropenia, usually with splenomegaly and increased susceptibility to infection.

Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (seco.description: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome that can be triggered by infections, malignancy, or autoimmune disease and may cause persistent fever and severe cytopenias. Visceral leishmaniasis is a recognized trigger.

Necrobiosis lipoidica.description: A chronic granulomatous skin disorder strongly associated with diabetes mellitus, characterized by slowly enlarging yellow-brown to reddish plaques on the shins with central atrophy, telangiectasia, and possible tenderness or ulceration. Histology typically shows necrobiotic collagen with palisading granulomatous inflammation.

Granuloma annulare.description: A benign inflammatory dermatosis consisting of dermal palisading granulomas, often presenting as annular papules or plaques on the extremities. Generalized forms may be associated with diabetes, but lesions are usually asymptomatic and lack the characteristic atrophic yellow center of necrobiosis lipoidica.

Diabetic dermopathy.description: A common diabetic microvascular skin finding causing small, round or oval, brown, atrophic macules on the shins, often called shin spots. They are typically multiple, asymptomatic, and do not progressively enlarge into inflammatory plaques.

Pretibial myxedema.description: Localized dermal accumulation of glycosaminoglycans, most often associated with Graves disease, causing nonpitting thickened plaques or nodules on the shins with an orange-peel texture. It is not typically associated with diabetes alone.

Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1B (PHP1B).description: A disorder of resistance to parathyroid hormone, usually caused by abnormal methylation at the GNAS locus. It produces hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and elevated parathyroid hormone despite adequate hormone production.

Hypocalcemic tetany due to parathyroid h.normalized_text: Hypocalcemic tetany due to parathyroid hormone resistance
Hypocalcemic tetany due to parathyroid h.description: Neuromuscular hyperexcitability caused by severe low serum calcium. In this case, the biochemical pattern suggests that the hypocalcemia is caused by resistance to parathyroid hormone.

Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A (PHP1A).description: A form of parathyroid hormone resistance caused by inactivating GNAS variants, typically associated with Albright hereditary osteodystrophy and resistance to other hormones such as thyroid-stimulating hormone.

Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorde.normalized_text: Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) triggered by choking fear
Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorde.description: An eating disorder characterized by restricted food intake due to fear of aversive consequences such as choking or vomiting, without body-image concerns. It may occur after a traumatic choking event.

Disseminated histoplasmosis.description: Systemic infection with Histoplasma capsulatum, often involving lungs, liver, spleen, lymph nodes, and bone marrow; tissue may show granulomatous inflammation containing small intracellular yeasts highlighted by fungal stains.
