Dabrafenib-trametinib–associated drug fe.description: Pyrexia is a common adverse effect of combined BRAF and MEK inhibitor therapy, particularly dabrafenib plus trametinib. Fever may be recurrent, high grade, and associated with nausea, rigors, dehydration, and tachycardia.

Disseminated tuberculosis.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis can cause prolonged fever and disseminated granulomatous disease involving the lungs, liver, spleen, and lymph nodes. Tissue classically shows caseating granulomas and acid-fast bacilli.

Sarcoidosis or sarcoid-like reaction rel.normalized_text: Sarcoidosis or sarcoid-like reaction related to BRAF/MEK inhibitor therapy
Sarcoidosis or sarcoid-like reaction rel.description: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous inflammatory disorder that may affect lungs, lymph nodes, liver, and spleen. BRAF/MEK inhibitors can rarely trigger sarcoid-like granulomatous reactions.

Metastatic melanoma with visceral and pu.normalized_text: Metastatic melanoma with visceral and pulmonary involvement
Metastatic melanoma with visceral and pu.description: Melanoma can recur after surgery and spread to lymph nodes, lungs, liver, spleen, bone, brain, and other organs. Advanced disease may produce constitutional symptoms and abdominal discomfort from liver involvement.

Pancreatic metastasis from prostate aden.description: Metastatic prostate cancer involving the pancreas can produce pancreatic duct or biliary obstruction, abdominal pain, pancreatitis, and cholestatic liver-enzyme abnormalities. It is uncommon but strongly supported by the history of metastatic prostate cancer and the pancreatic mass sampled by endoscopic ultrasound.

Acute pancreatitis due to pancreatic or.normalized_text: Acute pancreatitis due to pancreatic or biliary obstruction
Acute pancreatitis due to pancreatic or.description: Acute pancreatitis is inflammation of the pancreas, commonly caused by gallstones, alcohol, medications, or obstruction from a pancreatic lesion. Obstruction from metastatic disease or another mass could explain an episode of pancreatitis.

Acute cholecystitis.description: Acute cholecystitis is inflammation of the gallbladder, usually caused by obstruction of the cystic duct by gallstones, sludge, or less commonly tumor-related obstruction.

Malignant biliary obstruction from pancr.normalized_text: Malignant biliary obstruction from pancreatic malignancy
Malignant biliary obstruction from pancr.description: A pancreatic mass, whether primary pancreatic adenocarcinoma or metastatic cancer, can obstruct the common bile duct and cause cholestatic liver-test abnormalities, gallbladder distention, and upper abdominal pain.

Allgrove syndrome (Triple-A syndrome; ac.normalized_text: Allgrove syndrome (Triple-A syndrome; achalasia-alacrima-adrenal insufficiency syndrome)
Allgrove syndrome (Triple-A syndrome; ac.description: An autosomal recessive disorder, usually caused by AAAS gene variants, characterized by alacrima, achalasia/dysphagia, ACTH-resistant primary adrenal insufficiency, and progressive neurologic/autonomic dysfunction.

4A syndrome (Allgrove syndrome with neur.description: A neurologic form of Allgrove syndrome in which the classic Triple-A features occur with progressive autonomic neuropathy, pyramidal signs, peripheral neuropathy or amyotrophy, bulbar dysfunction, and sometimes intellectual disability.

X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy.description: A peroxisomal disorder causing adrenal insufficiency and progressive neurologic disease, including spastic paraparesis, ataxia, cognitive decline, and peripheral neuropathy. Elevated very-long-chain fatty acids are expected in typical cases.

Familial glucocorticoid deficiency.description: A group of inherited disorders causing isolated glucocorticoid deficiency with high ACTH, hyperpigmentation, hypoglycemia, and recurrent illness, while mineralocorticoid function is generally preserved.

Cerebral fat embolism syndrome related t.normalized_text: Cerebral fat embolism syndrome related to bone marrow necrosis from metastatic breast cancer
Cerebral fat embolism syndrome related t.description: Cerebral fat embolism is occlusion of cerebral microvessels by fat droplets, often producing a diffuse encephalopathy and a 'starfield' pattern of multiple diffusion-restricted lesions with microhemorrhages on MRI. In metastatic cancer, marrow infiltration or bone marrow necrosis can release marrow fat even without trauma.

Cancer-associated multifocal embolic isc.normalized_text: Cancer-associated multifocal embolic ischemic strokes (Trousseau syndrome)
Cancer-associated multifocal embolic isc.description: Advanced malignancy can cause a hypercoagulable state leading to recurrent or multifocal arterial thromboemboli and ischemic strokes in multiple vascular territories, sometimes with hemorrhagic transformation.

Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis wit.normalized_text: Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis with cerebral emboli
Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis wit.description: Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis involves sterile platelet-fibrin vegetations on cardiac valves, most often in patients with advanced malignancy. Embolization can cause multiple acute ischemic strokes in different cerebral territories.

Cerebral thrombotic microangiopathy asso.normalized_text: Cerebral thrombotic microangiopathy associated with malignancy
Cerebral thrombotic microangiopathy asso.description: Cancer-associated thrombotic microangiopathy can produce widespread small-vessel thrombosis, ischemic brain injury, encephalopathy, and occasionally hemorrhagic lesions. It may occur in advanced metastatic cancer or with certain cancer therapies.

Posterior reversible encephalopathy synd.description: PRES is a neurotoxic syndrome characterized by vasogenic edema, usually involving posterior cerebral regions, causing altered mental status, seizures, headache, and visual symptoms. It may occur with cancer therapy, renal dysfunction, hypertension, or endothelial injury.

Isolated intramedullary spinal neurosarc.description: A rare manifestation of sarcoidosis in which noncaseating granulomatous inflammation involves the spinal cord, producing an enhancing intramedullary cervical lesion and progressive myelopathy. Histology typically shows noncaseating granulomas with multinucleated giant cells and negative infectious stains.

Idiopathic transverse myelitis.description: An acute or subacute inflammatory spinal cord syndrome causing motor, sensory, and autonomic dysfunction below a spinal cord lesion, sometimes without an identifiable autoimmune, infectious, or systemic cause.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.description: An autoimmune inflammatory demyelinating disorder, commonly associated with aquaporin-4 antibodies, that can cause severe myelitis and optic neuritis. Spinal lesions often extend across three or more vertebral segments.

Multiple sclerosis with cervical myeliti.description: A chronic immune-mediated demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that may cause focal spinal cord lesions, sensory symptoms, weakness, spasticity, and bladder dysfunction.

Intramedullary spinal cord tumor (such a.normalized_text: Intramedullary spinal cord tumor (such as ependymoma or astrocytoma)
Intramedullary spinal cord tumor (such a.description: A primary tumor arising within the spinal cord that can produce progressive cervical myelopathy through cord expansion, tract dysfunction, and possible contrast enhancement.

Pulmonary actinomycosis.description: A chronic, suppurative lung infection caused by Actinomyces species, often producing mass-like consolidation, cavitation, abscess formation, and pleuritic chest pain. It may mimic malignancy or tuberculosis and can fail to respond to nonspecific short-course antibiotic treatment.

Bacterial lung abscess / necrotizing pne.description: A localized destructive bacterial infection of lung tissue that causes necrosis and cavitation, often with purulent sputum, focal crackles, and pleuritic chest pain. Aspiration-related anaerobic infection and Staphylococcus, Klebsiella, or other bacteria can cause this pattern.

Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (focal.description: An inflammatory lung disorder in which granulation tissue plugs form in distal airways and alveoli, often after a respiratory infection. It can present as persistent cough with focal consolidation and may be mistaken for bacterial pneumonia or cancer.

Pulmonary tuberculosis.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can cause persistent cough, sputum production, focal infiltrates, cavitation, and chest discomfort. Although classically upper-lobe predominant, lower-lobe disease may occur.

Primary lung cancer with post-obstructiv.normalized_text: Primary lung cancer with post-obstructive pneumonia
Primary lung cancer with post-obstructiv.description: A bronchial tumor can obstruct an airway and lead to retained secretions, recurrent infection, focal consolidation, and cavitation. Smoking is a risk factor, although primary lung cancer is less common at age 33.

Subcutaneous dirofilariasis due to Dirof.normalized_text: Subcutaneous dirofilariasis due to Dirofilaria repens
Subcutaneous dirofilariasis due to Dirof.description: A zoonotic filarial nematode infection transmitted by mosquitoes, usually from dogs. Humans are accidental hosts and typically develop a solitary painless subcutaneous nodule containing an immature worm.

Human sparganosis.description: Infection with migrating larval tapeworms of Spirometra species, which can produce slowly migrating subcutaneous nodules after ingestion of contaminated water or exposure to infected amphibians or reptiles.

Subcutaneous cysticercosis.description: Tissue infection with larval Taenia solium cysts. It may cause painless, mobile subcutaneous nodules, sometimes with associated neurocysticercosis.

Loiasis.description: A filarial infection caused by Loa loa, characterized by transient migrating subcutaneous swellings (Calabar swellings) and sometimes visible migration of worms across the eye.

Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), Ri.description: A progressive tau-related neurodegenerative disorder characterized by early postural instability and falls, axial-predominant parkinsonism, vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, dysarthria, dysphagia, and cognitive/behavioral changes.

Multiple system atrophy (MSA), parkinson.normalized_text: Multiple system atrophy (MSA), parkinsonian or cerebellar phenotype
Multiple system atrophy (MSA), parkinson.description: A rapidly progressive synucleinopathy causing autonomic failure with parkinsonism and/or cerebellar ataxia; eye movement abnormalities and dysphagia may occur, but a classic vertical supranuclear gaze palsy is less typical.

Corticobasal syndrome (CBS) / corticobas.description: A neurodegenerative tauopathy syndrome featuring asymmetric parkinsonism, limb apraxia, cortical sensory deficits, myoclonus, dystonia, and sometimes eye movement abnormalities or speech impairment.

Niemann-Pick disease type C, adult-onset.normalized_text: Niemann-Pick disease type C, adult-onset form
Niemann-Pick disease type C, adult-onset.description: A lysosomal lipid-storage disorder that can present in adulthood with vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, ataxia, dystonia, dysphagia, psychiatric symptoms, and progressive cognitive decline.

Whipple disease with oculomasticatory/oc.normalized_text: Whipple disease with oculomasticatory/oculofacioskeletal myorhythmia or CNS involvement
Whipple disease with oculomasticatory/oc.description: A rare infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei that may involve the central nervous system and cause eye movement abnormalities, ataxia, supranuclear gaze palsy, cognitive changes, and characteristic rhythmic facial or masticatory movements.

Cryptococcal meningitis due to Cryptococ.normalized_text: Cryptococcal meningitis due to Cryptococcus neoformans
Cryptococcal meningitis due to Cryptococ.description: Opportunistic fungal meningitis caused by encapsulated Cryptococcus yeast, most commonly occurring in advanced HIV/AIDS. The images are consistent with encapsulated budding yeasts seen with India ink staining and mucicarmine staining.

Tuberculous meningitis.description: A subacute or chronic meningitis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, often producing lymphocytic CSF inflammation, elevated protein, low glucose, and increased intracranial pressure. It is more common in severe immunosuppression.

Viral meningitis or meningoencephalitis.description: Inflammation of the meninges, sometimes with brain involvement, caused by viruses such as enteroviruses, herpes simplex virus, varicella-zoster virus, or HIV itself. CSF usually shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose.

Acute bacterial meningitis.description: An acute infection of the meninges caused by bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae or Neisseria meningitidis, usually characterized by fever, headache, neck stiffness, altered mental status, neutrophilic CSF pleocytosis, high protein, and low CSF glucose.

Neurosyphilis with syphilitic meningitis.description: Central nervous system involvement by Treponema pallidum, which can cause aseptic meningitis, headache, cranial neuropathies, and lymphocytic CSF pleocytosis. Risk is increased among sexually active men with HIV.

Acute ischemic infarction of the left me.normalized_text: Acute ischemic infarction of the left medial longitudinal fasciculus (internuclear ophthalmoplegia due to pontine stroke)
Acute ischemic infarction of the left me.description: A small ischemic stroke affecting the medial longitudinal fasciculus in the pons disrupts coordination between the abducens and oculomotor nuclei, producing internuclear ophthalmoplegia.

Left internuclear ophthalmoplegia.description: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia is an eye-movement disorder caused by damage to the medial longitudinal fasciculus, characterized by impaired adduction of the ipsilateral eye and abducting nystagmus of the opposite eye.

Posterior circulation ischemic stroke.description: An ischemic stroke in the vertebrobasilar circulation can affect the pons or midbrain and produce isolated ocular motor abnormalities, including internuclear ophthalmoplegia.

Multiple sclerosis causing internuclear.description: Multiple sclerosis can cause demyelination of the medial longitudinal fasciculus and is a classic cause of internuclear ophthalmoplegia, often with diplopia and impaired eye adduction.

Congenital babesiosis (Babesia microti i.description: A tick-borne intraerythrocytic protozoal infection that can rarely be transmitted transplacentally or perinatally. It causes hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, fever, and splenomegaly; blood smears may show ring forms and tetrads (Maltese-cross forms) within red cells.

Congenital malaria, especially Plasmodiu.normalized_text: Congenital malaria, especially Plasmodium falciparum infection
Congenital malaria, especially Plasmodiu.description: Malaria is a protozoal infection of red blood cells that may be congenitally transmitted from mother to infant. P. falciparum can produce multiple delicate ring forms in individual erythrocytes and may cause severe hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, and critical illness.

Neonatal bacterial sepsis with dissemina.normalized_text: Neonatal bacterial sepsis with disseminated intravascular coagulation
Neonatal bacterial sepsis with dissemina.description: Sepsis in a young infant can cause fever, lethargy, respiratory distress, poor perfusion, thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy, and multiorgan injury. Disseminated intravascular coagulation may cause elevated D-dimer and thrombocytopenia.

Metastatic recurrent prostate adenocarci.normalized_text: Metastatic recurrent prostate adenocarcinoma with rectal involvement
Metastatic recurrent prostate adenocarci.description: Late recurrence of high-grade prostate cancer after prostatectomy, with metastatic spread to sites such as lung and liver and possible local pelvic/rectal invasion causing tenesmus and pain.

Primary rectal adenocarcinoma with metas.normalized_text: Primary rectal adenocarcinoma with metastatic disease
Primary rectal adenocarcinoma with metas.description: Cancer arising in the rectum can cause painful defecation, tenesmus, weight loss, and fatigue; advanced disease may metastasize to the liver and lungs.

Pelvic metastatic malignancy causing rec.normalized_text: Pelvic metastatic malignancy causing rectal compression or invasion
Pelvic metastatic malignancy causing rec.description: Metastatic cancer in the pelvis, including recurrent prostate cancer or another pelvic malignancy, can compress or invade the rectum and produce severe tenesmus and rectal pain along with constitutional symptoms.

Thyrotoxic hypokalemic periodic paralysi.normalized_text: Thyrotoxic hypokalemic periodic paralysis due to Graves disease
Thyrotoxic hypokalemic periodic paralysi.description: A potentially life-threatening complication of thyrotoxicosis in which potassium shifts into skeletal muscle cells, causing severe hypokalemia and acute flaccid weakness. Graves disease is supported by diffuse hypervascular thyroid imaging and lymphocytic thyroid pathology.

Graves disease with thyrotoxicosis.description: An autoimmune disorder in which thyroid-stimulating antibodies cause diffuse thyroid overactivity, often producing diffuse goiter, increased thyroid blood flow, tremor, weight loss, gastrointestinal hypermotility, and eye findings.

Supplement-associated thyrotoxicosis or.normalized_text: Supplement-associated thyrotoxicosis or exacerbation of underlying Graves disease
Supplement-associated thyrotoxicosis or.description: Herbal or dietary supplements may contain thyroid hormone, iodine, stimulants, or other substances that can trigger or worsen thyrotoxicosis; in a patient with underlying Graves disease, this can precipitate thyrotoxic periodic paralysis.

Familial hypokalemic periodic paralysis.description: An inherited skeletal-muscle channel disorder causing episodic weakness due to intracellular potassium shifts, often precipitated by carbohydrate intake, exercise, stress, or medications.

Hypokalemic weakness from gastrointestin.normalized_text: Hypokalemic weakness from gastrointestinal potassium loss
Hypokalemic weakness from gastrointestin.description: Diarrhea can cause potassium depletion and metabolic acidosis, leading to muscle weakness, cramps, and in severe cases paralysis.

Torus palatinus.description: A benign bony exostosis arising from the midline of the hard palate. It is usually asymptomatic, covered by normal mucosa, and may be lobulated or very large.

Palatal osteoma.description: A benign, slow-growing tumor composed of mature bone that can present as a painless, firm mass of the palate or other craniofacial bones.

Congenital palatal hamartoma.description: A benign developmental overgrowth of normal tissue components in the palate. Such lesions may be present from birth and can remain stable or slowly enlarge over many years.

diagnoses.name: Intervertebral disc prolapse
diagnoses.icd11_title: Intervertebral disc degeneration without prolapsed disc with determinant

Lumbar intervertebral disc herniation wi.normalized_text: Lumbar intervertebral disc herniation with radiculopathy
Lumbar intervertebral disc herniation wi.description: Displacement of lumbar disc material that compresses a nerve root, commonly causing sciatica and motor weakness. The MRI appearance is compatible with degenerative lumbar disc disease and a lower-lumbar disc protrusion/extrusion.

Lumbar spinal stenosis due to degenerati.normalized_text: Lumbar spinal stenosis due to degenerative disc disease
Lumbar spinal stenosis due to degenerati.description: Narrowing of the lumbar spinal canal or lateral recesses from disc degeneration, disc bulging, facet arthropathy, or ligament thickening, which may compress nerve roots.

Lumbar epidural venous varix or thrombos.normalized_text: Lumbar epidural venous varix or thrombosed epidural varix
Lumbar epidural venous varix or thrombos.description: An enlarged or thrombosed epidural venous plexus can compress a lumbar nerve root and mimic a herniated disc on MRI, producing acute radicular pain and weakness.

Lumbar facet synovial cyst.description: A fluid-containing cyst arising from a degenerative facet joint that may extend into the spinal canal or neural foramen and compress a lumbar nerve root.

Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (H.normalized_text: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) with cardiac and cerebral involvement
Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (H.description: A disorder characterized by persistent marked eosinophilia causing eosinophil-mediated injury and thrombosis in organs such as the heart, brain, lungs, skin, and peripheral nerves after secondary causes have been excluded.

Eosinophilic myocarditis due to hypereos.normalized_text: Eosinophilic myocarditis due to hypereosinophilic syndrome
Eosinophilic myocarditis due to hypereos.description: Inflammatory myocardial injury caused by eosinophilic infiltration, which may lead to myocardial necrosis, ventricular dysfunction, mural thrombus formation, and systemic embolic events including stroke.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyang.normalized_text: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA, Churg-Strauss syndrome)
Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyang.description: A necrotizing eosinophil-rich small- and medium-vessel vasculitis that commonly causes asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis, eosinophilia, pulmonary infiltrates, neuropathy, and cardiac involvement.

Chronic eosinophilic leukemia or another.normalized_text: Chronic eosinophilic leukemia or another clonal myeloid hypereosinophilic neoplasm
Chronic eosinophilic leukemia or another.description: A hematologic neoplasm in which clonal eosinophil proliferation produces sustained marked eosinophilia and can cause tissue infiltration, thrombosis, cardiac injury, and neurologic complications.

Parasitic helminth infection with hypere.description: Helminthic infections can produce substantial eosinophilia and, depending on the organism, may cause pulmonary, gastrointestinal, neurologic, or cardiac disease.

Sarcoidosis.description: A multisystem granulomatous inflammatory disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas, commonly involving bilateral hilar/mediastinal lymph nodes and lungs.

Breast cancer recurrence with mediastina.normalized_text: Breast cancer recurrence with mediastinal and pulmonary metastases
Breast cancer recurrence with mediastina.description: Recurrent breast carcinoma may spread to intrathoracic lymph nodes, lungs, bone, liver, or other organs and can produce FDG-avid lesions on PET imaging.

Tuberculous lymphadenitis or pulmonary t.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can cause granulomatous inflammation, thoracic lymph-node enlargement, pulmonary infiltrates or nodules, and increased FDG uptake.

Lymphoma.description: Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphomas can cause FDG-avid mediastinal lymphadenopathy, systemic cytopenias, and pulmonary involvement.

Symptomatic multiple myeloma (IgG kappa.description: A malignant plasma-cell disorder producing a monoclonal immunoglobulin and/or free light chains, causing bone-marrow infiltration and end-organ damage such as anemia, hypercalcemia, renal dysfunction, and lytic bone disease.

Smoldering multiple myeloma.description: An asymptomatic plasma-cell neoplasm with a substantial monoclonal protein and/or marrow plasma-cell burden but without myeloma-defining end-organ damage or biomarker-defined active disease.

Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined si.description: A precursor condition characterized by a small monoclonal protein without substantial clonal plasma-cell infiltration, end-organ injury, or myeloma-defining events.

Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia / lymphopl.description: A lymphoplasmacytic B-cell lymphoma that usually secretes IgM monoclonal protein and may cause anemia, hyperviscosity, neuropathy, lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly.

Metastatic bone malignancy with incident.normalized_text: Metastatic bone malignancy with incidental monoclonal gammopathy
Metastatic bone malignancy with incident.description: Metastatic solid tumors can infiltrate bone marrow and cause anemia, hypercalcemia, elevated inflammatory markers, renal dysfunction, and destructive or sclerotic bone lesions.

Bifocal intracranial germinoma (suprasel.normalized_text: Bifocal intracranial germinoma (suprasellar and pineal germinoma)
Bifocal intracranial germinoma (suprasel.description: A germ-cell tumor that commonly affects adolescent and young adult males and may involve both the pineal and suprasellar regions. Suprasellar involvement can cause diabetes insipidus, visual pathway compression, and pituitary hormone deficiencies.

Craniopharyngioma.description: A benign epithelial tumor of the sellar and suprasellar region that can compress the pituitary stalk, optic chiasm, and hypothalamus, causing visual symptoms, diabetes insipidus, and multiple pituitary hormone deficiencies.

Pituitary macroadenoma causing panhypopi.description: A large pituitary adenoma may compress normal pituitary tissue and the optic chiasm, producing headache, visual disturbance, hypogonadism, and secondary hypothyroidism. Diabetes insipidus is uncommon because posterior pituitary involvement is unusual.

Langerhans cell histiocytosis with hypot.normalized_text: Langerhans cell histiocytosis with hypothalamic-pituitary involvement
Langerhans cell histiocytosis with hypot.description: A clonal histiocytic disorder that can infiltrate the pituitary stalk and hypothalamus. Central diabetes insipidus is a common endocrine manifestation, and anterior pituitary hormone deficiencies may develop.

Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aur.normalized_text: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus native aortic valve infective endocarditis with peri-aortic abscess
Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aur.description: Severe bacterial infection of the aortic valve caused by MRSA, with likely extension into peri-valvular tissue forming an aortic root abscess. This can cause aortic regurgitation, conduction abnormalities, and systemic embolization.

Aortic valve infective endocarditis caus.normalized_text: Aortic valve infective endocarditis causing severe aortic regurgitation
Aortic valve infective endocarditis caus.description: Infection of the aortic valve can damage valve leaflets and produce aortic regurgitation, typically heard as an early diastolic decrescendo murmur. Embolic and immunologic peripheral findings may occur.

Septic embolic ischemic stroke secondary.normalized_text: Septic embolic ischemic stroke secondary to infective endocarditis
Septic embolic ischemic stroke secondary.description: Fragments of infected valvular vegetation can embolize to cerebral arteries, causing ischemic stroke, focal neurologic deficits, and occasionally brain abscess or hemorrhagic transformation.

Perivalvular/aortic root abscess with co.normalized_text: Perivalvular/aortic root abscess with conduction system involvement
Perivalvular/aortic root abscess with co.description: A deep cardiac abscess adjacent to the aortic valve can extend into the interventricular septum and damage the conduction system, producing PR prolongation or higher-grade atrioventricular block. It is a serious complication of infective endocarditis.

Classic infantile-onset Pompe disease (a.normalized_text: Classic infantile-onset Pompe disease (acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency)
Classic infantile-onset Pompe disease (a.description: An autosomal-recessive lysosomal glycogen-storage disorder caused by deficiency of acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA), resulting in glycogen accumulation predominantly in cardiac, skeletal, and respiratory muscle. Classic infantile disease typically presents during the first months of life with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, hypotonia, muscle weakness, and elevated muscle enzymes.

Late-onset Pompe disease.description: A milder phenotypic spectrum of GAA deficiency with residual enzyme activity, usually presenting in childhood or adulthood with progressive proximal and respiratory muscle weakness and usually without severe infantile cardiomyopathy.

Danon disease.description: An X-linked lysosomal glycogen-storage/myopathy disorder caused by LAMP2 deficiency. It commonly causes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, skeletal myopathy, and variable intellectual or developmental impairment, particularly in males.

PRKAG2-related glycogen-storage cardiomy.description: An autosomal-dominant cardiac glycogen-storage disorder caused by PRKAG2 variants, characterized by hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, ventricular pre-excitation, and conduction-system disease; skeletal muscle involvement is generally limited.

Precursor B-cell acute lymphoblastic leu.normalized_text: Precursor B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoblastic lymphoma (B-ALL/LBL)
Precursor B-cell acute lymphoblastic leu.description: A malignant proliferation of immature B lymphoblasts involving bone marrow and sometimes extramedullary sites. It can cause bone pain, fever, limp, bruising, and soft-tissue or organ infiltration.

Neuroblastoma.description: A childhood cancer of sympathetic nervous system tissue, usually arising from the adrenal gland or abdominal sympathetic chain. It may metastasize to bone and bone marrow, causing bone pain, limp, fever, abdominal enlargement, and periorbital ecchymoses.

Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, including lymphobl.description: A group of lymphoid malignancies that can involve lymph nodes, bone marrow, bone, abdominal organs, and soft tissues. Pediatric lymphoma may present with fever, bone pain, limp, abdominal enlargement, and extranodal masses.

Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelit.normalized_text: Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis (CRMO) / chronic nonbacterial osteitis
Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelit.description: An autoinflammatory disorder causing recurrent sterile inflammation of multiple bones. It commonly affects children and causes episodic bone pain, limp, and lesions at multiple skeletal sites.

Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (.normalized_text: Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (systemic JIA/Still disease)
Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (.description: A childhood inflammatory rheumatologic disease characterized by arthritis with recurrent fever and systemic inflammation. Children may have joint pain, limp, and fever, although overt arthritis is usually present.

Cellulitis.description: Acute bacterial infection of the deeper dermis and subcutaneous tissue, typically causing diffuse erythema, warmth, tenderness, and swelling. Ultrasound may show subcutaneous edema with a cobblestone appearance and no drainable collection.

Erysipelas.description: A superficial bacterial skin infection, usually caused by streptococci, involving the upper dermis and lymphatic vessels. It produces painful erythema and edema, often with a relatively well-demarcated raised border.

Gluteal soft-tissue abscess.description: A localized collection of pus in the skin or subcutaneous tissues, commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus. It typically causes focal painful swelling, erythema, fluctuance, and may require drainage.

Necrotizing soft-tissue infection (early.description: A rapidly progressive, life-threatening infection of fascia and deep soft tissue. Early disease can resemble cellulitis, but typically progresses quickly with severe pain, systemic toxicity, skin discoloration, bullae, crepitus, or shock.

Gluteal hematoma or spontaneous soft-tis.normalized_text: Gluteal hematoma or spontaneous soft-tissue bleeding
Gluteal hematoma or spontaneous soft-tis.description: Bleeding into subcutaneous tissue or muscle can cause painful swelling and bruising, usually after trauma, anticoagulant use, strenuous exertion, or a bleeding disorder.

Chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGVHD.normalized_text: Chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGVHD), with sclerodermatous/fascial involvement
Chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGVHD.description: A late immune-mediated complication of allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation in which donor immune cells attack recipient tissues. Skin, fascia, liver, and muscles may be affected; sclerotic skin/fascial disease can cause joint contractures and a positive prayer sign.

Dermatomyositis.description: An inflammatory autoimmune myopathy characterized by proximal muscle weakness and characteristic photosensitive skin eruptions, often accompanied by elevated muscle enzymes and sometimes systemic manifestations.

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).description: A multisystem autoimmune disease that can cause photosensitive cutaneous eruptions, fever, musculoskeletal symptoms, positive ANA, and involvement of internal organs including the liver and kidneys.

Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma).description: An autoimmune connective-tissue disease characterized by progressive skin thickening and fibrosis, reduced joint mobility, and potential internal-organ involvement. Skin sclerosis can produce a prayer sign.

Multiple eruptive keratoacanthomas.description: A disorder characterized by the recurrent eruption of multiple rapidly growing keratotic papules or nodules, often with a central keratin-filled crater. Keratoacanthomas are considered part of the squamous-cell carcinoma spectrum and may occur more frequently in immunologically altered patients.

Generalized eruptive keratoacanthoma of.description: A rare variant of eruptive keratoacanthoma characterized by numerous disseminated small keratotic papules, often on sun-exposed skin, with severe itching and recurrent crops of lesions.

Multiple self-healing squamous epithelio.description: An inherited condition causing recurrent multiple keratoacanthoma-like squamous tumors that typically grow rapidly and then involute, often leaving scars.

Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, kerat.description: A keratinocyte skin cancer that may present as a rapidly growing hyperkeratotic, crusted, or ulcerated papule or nodule. Keratoacanthoma-type lesions can be difficult to distinguish histologically and clinically from conventional cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma.

Acquired perforating dermatosis associat.normalized_text: Acquired perforating dermatosis associated with chronic renal failure and hemodialysis
Acquired perforating dermatosis associat.description: A pruritic perforating skin disorder seen commonly in patients with diabetes or chronic kidney failure on dialysis. It causes excoriated hyperkeratotic papules and nodules, often on the extremities, due to transepidermal elimination of dermal material.

Zika virus-associated acute transverse m.description: Acute inflammatory injury of the spinal cord caused by Zika virus infection, producing motor weakness, sensory deficits with a spinal sensory level, pain, and autonomic dysfunction such as urinary retention.

Acute transverse myelitis.description: A syndrome of acute spinal cord inflammation causing bilateral or asymmetric weakness, sensory impairment below a spinal level, pain, and bladder or bowel dysfunction. It may be post-infectious, autoimmune, or infection-associated.

Longitudinally extensive transverse myel.description: A severe form of transverse myelitis involving a long segment of the spinal cord, often associated with viral infection, neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, or other inflammatory conditions.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder.description: An autoimmune inflammatory disorder that can cause longitudinally extensive myelitis and optic neuritis. It is usually associated with aquaporin-4 or myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibodies, though antibody-negative cases occur.

Multiple sclerosis.description: A chronic immune-mediated demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that can cause focal weakness, sensory symptoms, myelitis, and bladder dysfunction, typically with episodes separated in time and lesions disseminated in the brain and spinal cord.

Guillain-Barre syndrome.description: An acute immune-mediated peripheral polyradiculoneuropathy, sometimes triggered by Zika virus, that usually causes progressive symmetric flaccid weakness, reduced reflexes, and variable sensory symptoms.

T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymp.normalized_text: T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (T-ALL/LBL), likely with TCRAD-associated rearrangement
T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymp.description: An aggressive precursor T-cell neoplasm involving bone marrow and blood, commonly presenting with circulating blasts, cytopenias, high LDH, and sometimes leukostasis or central nervous system symptoms. T-cell markers are expressed, although some cases lack TdT and CD34.

T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (T-PLL).description: A mature post-thymic T-cell leukemia characterized by marked lymphocytosis and expression of mature T-cell antigens, usually CD2, CD3, CD5, and CD7. It most often affects older adults and commonly causes splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and skin involvement.

Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL).description: A mature peripheral T-cell malignancy caused by human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1). Acute ATLL can present with leukemic blood involvement, high LDH, cytopenias, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, skin lesions, and hypercalcemia.

Early T-cell precursor acute lymphoblast.normalized_text: Early T-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ETP-ALL)
Early T-cell precursor acute lymphoblast.description: A high-risk immunophenotypic subtype of T-ALL arising from very immature thymic T-cell precursors. It typically lacks CD1a and CD8, has weak or absent CD5, and often expresses stem-cell or myeloid markers such as CD34, CD117, CD13, or CD33.

Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocyt.description: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome caused by uncontrolled activation of macrophages and lymphocytes, producing cytokine storm, hemophagocytosis, cytopenias, hypofibrinogenemia, and extreme hyperferritinemia.

Tuberculosis-associated hemophagocytic l.description: Secondary HLH triggered by active Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, often disseminated or severe pulmonary tuberculosis. It may cause prolonged fever, lung infiltrates, hepatosplenomegaly, marrow hemophagocytosis, cytopenias, and very high ferritin.

Disseminated tuberculosis.description: Widespread infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis involving multiple organs, potentially including lungs, liver, spleen, and bone marrow. Disseminated TB can precipitate HLH and severe respiratory failure.

Epstein-Barr virus-associated hemophagoc.description: A common infection-associated form of secondary HLH caused by EBV-driven immune activation. It frequently presents with persistent fever, cytopenias, liver/spleen enlargement, coagulopathy, and markedly elevated ferritin.

Severe bacterial sepsis with disseminate.normalized_text: Severe bacterial sepsis with disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
Severe bacterial sepsis with disseminate.description: A severe systemic infection can cause shock, acute respiratory distress syndrome, thrombocytopenia, low fibrinogen, and multiorgan dysfunction. Sepsis can also overlap with or trigger secondary HLH.

Japanese encephalitis.description: A mosquito-borne flaviviral encephalitis acquired in endemic parts of Asia and the western Pacific, causing fever, altered consciousness, seizures, and focal neurologic deficits.

Dengue encephalitis with cerebral vascul.normalized_text: Dengue encephalitis with cerebral vasculopathy or ischemic complications
Dengue encephalitis with cerebral vascul.description: Neurologic involvement from dengue virus infection can cause encephalitis, altered mental status, seizures, rash, and occasionally vascular complications such as ischemic stroke or cerebral venous thrombosis.

West Nile virus neuroinvasive disease.description: A mosquito-borne flavivirus infection that may cause meningitis, encephalitis, acute flaccid paralysis, coma, and focal neurologic abnormalities, especially in older adults.

Varicella-zoster virus encephalitis with.normalized_text: Varicella-zoster virus encephalitis with cerebral vasculopathy
Varicella-zoster virus encephalitis with.description: Varicella-zoster virus can produce encephalitis and inflammatory vasculopathy involving cerebral arteries, leading to multifocal ischemic strokes, focal deficits, and altered consciousness; it may occur with or without a typical vesicular rash.

Acute bacterial meningitis with meningov.normalized_text: Acute bacterial meningitis with meningovascular cerebral infarction
Acute bacterial meningitis with meningov.description: Bacterial meningitis can cause fever, coma, neutrophilic CSF inflammation, cerebral vasculitis, arterial thrombosis, and ischemic strokes with focal neurologic deficits.

IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura.description: An immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis characterized by IgA deposition, often triggered by an upper respiratory infection and presenting with palpable purpura, arthralgia or arthritis, gastrointestinal disease, and possible kidney involvement.

Cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis.description: A small-vessel inflammatory vasculitis of the skin that causes palpable purpura, most often on dependent lower extremities; it can follow infection, medications, autoimmune disease, or inflammatory bowel disease.

Adalimumab-associated immune-complex vas.description: A drug-induced small-vessel vasculitis that can occur during treatment with tumor necrosis factor-alpha inhibitors such as adalimumab, commonly producing palpable purpura and sometimes systemic immune-complex manifestations.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis.description: An ANCA-associated necrotizing vasculitis involving small and medium vessels, classically causing chronic sinonasal disease, pulmonary symptoms, kidney disease, and sometimes purpura or arthritis.

Deep venous thrombosis of the left lower.normalized_text: Deep venous thrombosis of the left lower extremity
Deep venous thrombosis of the left lower.description: Formation of a blood clot in a deep leg vein causing acute unilateral calf pain and swelling; inflammatory bowel disease and recent travel can increase thrombotic risk.

HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamous ce.normalized_text: HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma with cervical lymph-node metastasis
HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamous ce.description: A squamous cell cancer arising in the tonsil or base of tongue/oropharynx, often related to human papillomavirus (HPV). It commonly occurs in nonsmokers and may first present with a metastatic upper-neck lymph node.

Non-HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamou.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the oropharynx, including the tonsil or tongue base, that can spread to upper cervical lymph nodes. Traditional risk factors include tobacco and heavy alcohol exposure.

Oropharyngeal lymphoma.description: Lymphoma can involve Waldeyer's ring, including the palatine or lingual tonsils, and can cause a pharyngeal mass with cervical lymph-node enlargement.

Chronic cervical lymphadenitis from head.normalized_text: Chronic cervical lymphadenitis from head-and-neck infection
Chronic cervical lymphadenitis from head.description: Reactive or infectious enlargement of cervical lymph nodes may occur with chronic tonsillitis, dental infection, tuberculosis, or other upper aerodigestive infections.

Primary extranodal marginal zone B-cell.normalized_text: Primary extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT lymphoma) of the urinary bladder
Primary extranodal marginal zone B-cell.description: A rare indolent B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma arising in the bladder, often associated with chronic cystitis and persistent antigenic stimulation. It commonly remains localized and may lack systemic manifestations.

Chronic cystitis with reactive lymphoid.normalized_text: Chronic cystitis with reactive lymphoid follicular hyperplasia
Chronic cystitis with reactive lymphoid.description: Chronic inflammation of the bladder caused by recurrent infection can produce lymphoid aggregates and follicular cystitis, which may mimic lymphoma histologically or cystoscopically.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the uri.normalized_text: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the urinary bladder
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the uri.description: An aggressive B-cell lymphoma that can involve the bladder either as primary disease or as part of systemic lymphoma. It usually shows larger atypical lymphoid cells and often causes more rapidly progressive symptoms than MALT lymphoma.

Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder with.normalized_text: Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder with prominent inflammatory infiltrate
Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder with.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the bladder that commonly occurs in older adults and may present with urinary symptoms or recurrent urinary tract infections. Histology would show malignant urothelial cells rather than a clonal lymphoid infiltrate.

Left femoral neck fracture.description: A fracture through the neck of the femur, commonly occurring after a fall in frail older adults with osteoporosis. The pelvic radiograph is concerning for a proximal left femoral neck fracture.

Intertrochanteric fracture of the left f.normalized_text: Intertrochanteric fracture of the left femur
Intertrochanteric fracture of the left f.description: A fracture through the proximal femur between the greater and lesser trochanters, typically caused by a fall in elderly patients and sometimes difficult to distinguish from a femoral neck fracture on a single radiograph.

Klebsiella pneumoniae urinary tract infe.description: A bacterial urinary tract infection caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae. Older adults, particularly those with diabetes and dementia, may present with nonspecific symptoms such as weakness, confusion, or falls rather than urinary complaints.

Osteochondritis dissecans of the femoral.normalized_text: Osteochondritis dissecans of the femoral condyle with a detached osteochondral fragment
Osteochondritis dissecans of the femoral.description: A focal disorder of subchondral bone and overlying cartilage, usually affecting the medial femoral condyle in young active males. An unstable or detached fragment may become an intra-articular loose body and cause mechanical symptoms.

Intra-articular osteochondral loose body.description: A free fragment of bone and cartilage within the knee joint, commonly resulting from osteochondritis dissecans, prior osteochondral injury, or degenerative joint disease. It can intermittently obstruct joint movement.

Synovial chondromatosis.description: A benign proliferative disorder of synovium that forms cartilaginous nodules, which may calcify or ossify and detach into the joint as loose bodies. It commonly causes recurrent swelling, pain, and locking.

diagnoses.name: Primary pancreatic T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: Primary pancreatic T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma

Primary pancreatic diffuse large B-cell.normalized_text: Primary pancreatic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
Primary pancreatic diffuse large B-cell.description: A rare extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma arising in the pancreas, most often diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, which can form a pancreatic head mass and obstruct the bile duct.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the pancreatic ducts, commonly arising in the pancreatic head and causing extrahepatic biliary obstruction.

Distal cholangiocarcinoma.description: Cancer of the distal extrahepatic bile duct that produces progressive obstruction of bile flow and may appear as a mass near the pancreatic head.

Autoimmune pancreatitis with biliary obs.description: An immune-mediated inflammatory pancreatic disorder, often related to IgG4 disease, that can enlarge the pancreatic head and mimic pancreatic cancer by compressing the distal common bile duct.

Tumoral calcinosis secondary to chronic.normalized_text: Tumoral calcinosis secondary to chronic renal failure (uremic tumoral calcinosis)
Tumoral calcinosis secondary to chronic.description: Periarticular or subcutaneous deposition of calcium-phosphate material forming large, lobulated calcified masses, often occurring in long-term dialysis patients with hyperphosphatemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism.

Metastatic calcification due to calcium-.normalized_text: Metastatic calcification due to calcium-phosphate imbalance in end-stage renal disease
Metastatic calcification due to calcium-.description: Deposition of calcium salts in otherwise normal soft tissues due to systemic mineral metabolism abnormalities, particularly hyperphosphatemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism in renal failure.

Calcinosis cutis.description: Deposition of insoluble calcium salts in the skin or subcutaneous tissue. In this patient, a metabolic subtype related to renal failure and hyperphosphatemia would be most relevant.

Secondary hyperparathyroidism of chronic.normalized_text: Secondary hyperparathyroidism of chronic kidney disease with extraskeletal calcification
Secondary hyperparathyroidism of chronic.description: A chronic kidney disease-mineral and bone disorder in which phosphate retention, impaired vitamin D activation, and hypocalcemia stimulate parathyroid hormone secretion, promoting bone and soft-tissue complications.

Myositis ossificans.description: A benign heterotopic bone-forming lesion in soft tissue, usually after trauma, surgery, neurologic injury, or repeated tissue injury; it may present as a firm enlarging mass with peripheral ossification.

Lateral tibial plateau fracture (split-d.normalized_text: Lateral tibial plateau fracture (split-depression type, Schatzker II)
Lateral tibial plateau fracture (split-d.description: An intra-articular fracture of the lateral upper tibia involving a split component and depression of the articular surface; commonly occurs after high-energy valgus or axial loading trauma.

Tibial plateau fracture with associated.normalized_text: Tibial plateau fracture with associated hemarthrosis
Tibial plateau fracture with associated.description: A fracture extending into the knee joint can cause bleeding into the joint space, producing rapid swelling and painful limitation of weight bearing.

Anterior cruciate ligament injury associ.normalized_text: Anterior cruciate ligament injury associated with tibial plateau fracture
Anterior cruciate ligament injury associ.description: ACL tears can accompany high-energy tibial plateau fractures, particularly when the injury mechanism includes valgus stress, rotation, or anterior translation of the tibia.

Meniscal injury associated with lateral.normalized_text: Meniscal injury associated with lateral tibial plateau fracture
Meniscal injury associated with lateral.description: Lateral meniscal tears are frequently associated with lateral tibial plateau fractures because the meniscus can be trapped or injured by depression and displacement of the articular surface.

diagnoses.icd11_title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of unspecified gastrointestinal sites

Rectal gastrointestinal stromal tumor (G.description: A rare mesenchymal tumor of the gastrointestinal tract arising from interstitial cells of Cajal or related precursor cells. Rectal GISTs are commonly submucosal, composed of spindle cells, and often show KIT and/or DOG1 immunoreactivity with KIT or PDGFRA mutations.

Rectal leiomyoma.description: A benign smooth-muscle tumor that can arise from the muscularis mucosae or muscularis propria of the rectum. It generally presents as a circumscribed submucosal mass and may cause obstructive symptoms when large.

Rectal leiomyosarcoma.description: A malignant smooth-muscle tumor of the rectum. It can form a submucosal or intramural mass and may produce pain, constipation, tenesmus, bleeding, or obstructive symptoms.

Rectal schwannoma.description: An uncommon usually benign peripheral nerve-sheath tumor arising in the gastrointestinal wall. Rectal schwannomas are generally slow-growing, well-circumscribed submucosal masses that can cause obstructive symptoms.

Rectal endometriosis (deep infiltrating.description: Ectopic endometrial tissue involving the rectovaginal septum or bowel wall, usually in women of reproductive age. It may cause rectal pain, constipation, tenesmus, and an infiltrative rectal-wall mass.

SHORT syndrome (PIK3R1-related disorder).description: A rare autosomal dominant developmental disorder caused by pathogenic variants in PIK3R1. SHORT stands for short stature, hyperextensibility/hernia, ocular depression, Rieger anomaly, and teething delay; affected individuals often have intrauterine growth restriction, characteristic triangular facial appearance, lipoatrophy, thin skin, and delayed bone age.

Silver-Russell syndrome.description: A growth-restriction syndrome usually caused by abnormal imprinting at chromosome 11p15 or maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 7. It is characterized by prenatal and postnatal growth failure, relative macrocephaly, triangular face, prominent forehead, feeding difficulty, and body asymmetry in some children.

Cockayne syndrome.description: A rare DNA-repair disorder, usually caused by biallelic ERCC6 or ERCC8 variants, with postnatal growth failure, progressive neurologic impairment, photosensitivity, cachectic appearance, retinal disease, and sensorineural hearing loss.

Congenital generalized lipodystrophy.description: A group of genetic disorders characterized by near-complete lack of adipose tissue from birth or early infancy, resulting in a muscular appearance, prominent veins, hepatomegaly, insulin resistance, hypertriglyceridemia, and sometimes growth abnormalities.
